Furthermore, the moderation results indicate that the strength of the positive relationship betw een Generative AI-supported learning and epistemic confidence increases as the students' critical thinking disposition increases. analysis.methods: This study employed a quantitatively driven mixed-methods design with an embedded qualitative component. Quantitative data constituted the primary strand of the study and were used to assess teachers’ research competence and the related questionnaire constructs before and after participation in the professional development program. Qualitative data were obtained from two open-ended questionnaire items administered at the same measurement points and were used to contextualize and further interpret patterns observed in the quantitative findings. The qualitative component was therefore not implemented as a separate follow-up phase developed after preliminary quantitative analysis. Instead, quantitative and qualitative data were collected within the same broader assessment procedure and integrated during interpretation. The open-ended responses provided additional insight into how teachers described the role of students’ social-emotional well-being and the potential use of AI in educational research. This design enabled numerical changes in the measured constructs to be considered alongside changes in participants’ reported perceptions and intended practices. The two strands were integrated primarily at the interpretation stage and in the development of the empirically informed conceptual model. The research process comprised two complementary components: a quantitative component based on the structured questionnaire and an embedded qualitative component based on the two open-ended questions administered at the same measurement points. In the quantitative component, the structured questionnaire was used to assess chemistry teachers’ research competence, their reported practices of monitoring students’ social-emotional well-being, their perceptions of students’ achievement emotions, and their readiness to integrate AI technologies into research and pedagogical practice. The quantitative data were used to describe the baseline levels of teachers’ research competence and the related questionnaire constructs, as well as to examine the relationships among these predefined measures. The embedded qualitative component involved analysis of participants’ responses to the two open-ended questionnaire items using qualitative content analysis. The purpose of this qualitative component was to provide additional insight into teachers’ professional needs, perceived challenges in conducting educational research, and their views on the opportunities and limitations of AI-assisted research. Integration of the quantitative and qualitative findings informed the development of a study-derived conceptual model illustrating the relationships among educational inquiry, teachers’ social-emotional monitoring practices, AI-supported research practices, and evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. The study was conducted during the 2025–2026 academic year in public secondary schools in the South Kazakhstan region. A total of 105 chemistry teachers participated in the study. Participants were selected using the purposive sampling method. The main selection criteria were the participants’ currently teaching chemistry in a general secondary school, teaching experience, and informed voluntary consent to participate in the study. The sample comprised teachers with diverse levels of professional experience, qualification categories, and teaching backgrounds, allowing the researchers to examine research competence across a broad range of professional contexts and career stages. Data were collected using a theory-informed questionnaire developed for the present study. The questionnaire constructs and item content were informed by established theoretical frameworks and previously published instruments addressing teachers’ research competence, social-emotional monitoring, achievement emotions, and the educational use of artificial intelligence. Items were adapted to the context of in-service chemistry teachers and aligned with the constructs specified a priori in the study framework. The questionnaire development process included several stages ( Table 1 ). First, the initial item pool was reviewed by five experts with complementary expertise in chemistry education, educational research methodology, teacher professional development, educational psychology, and digital technologies in education. The experts evaluated the conceptual relevance, clarity, comprehensibility, and correspondence of each item with the intended construct. Based on their feedback, several items were linguistically simplified, overlapping formulations were reduced, and terminology related to artificial intelligence and social-emotional monitoring was clarified to ensure consistent interpretation by school teachers. The response format and Likert-scale anchors were also standardized across the quantitative sections. Structure of the questionnaire, measured constructs, and theoretical foundations. Second, the revised questionnaire was pilot-tested with 18 chemistry teachers who met the general characteristics of the target population but were not included in the final study sample. The pilot administration was used to assess item comprehensibility, completion time, response consistency, and potential ambiguity in the instructions. Minor wording revisions were introduced after the pilot stage, particularly for items concerning research methodology, students’ achievement emotions, and the use of AI in educational research. No items were removed at this stage because the pilot responses indicated that the intended constructs were understandable to participants. The questionnaire administered in the study was prepared and delivered in Kazakh, which was the working language of the participating teachers. Because the final questionnaire items were adapted and formulated directly in Kazakh rather than translated verbatim from a single foreign-language instrument, a conventional forward–backward translation procedure was not applied to the complete questionnaire. However, where theoretical constructs and terminology originated from English-language sources, two bilingual researchers independently compared the Kazakh wording with the original conceptual definitions and resolved wording differences through discussion. This procedure was used to preserve conceptual rather than literal equivalence between the source frameworks and the Kazakh-language items. analysis.discussion: The present study examined changes in chemistry teachers’ research competence following participation in an AI-supported professional development program integrating teacher inquiry, social-emotional monitoring, and AI. The combined quantitative and qualitative findings showed that research competence can be understood as a multidimensional and integrated professional construct encompassing inquiry, evidence interpretation, reflective practice, and data-informed pedagogical decision-making. Statistically significant pre–post improvements were observed across the measured constructs, while the qualitative findings indicated corresponding shifts in teachers’ perceptions and reported practices. These patterns suggest that participation in the program was associated with greater integration of educational research into teachers’ instructional practice and with increased attention to evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. Regarding the first research question, the descriptive findings characterized the baseline levels of teachers’ research competence and the related constructs predefined in the questionnaire. Among these measures, teachers’ research competence showed the lowest mean item score, whereas comparatively higher baseline scores were observed for social-emotional monitoring and perceptions of achievement emotions. Correlation analysis further revealed statistically significant positive associations among research competence, research engagement, social-emotional monitoring, achievement emotions, and readiness to use AI. These relationships indicate that the measured constructs are associated within teachers’ broader professional practice; however, they should not be interpreted as evidence that the present study empirically established the internal dimensional structure of research competence. The constructs were specified a priori on the basis of the theoretical framework and previous research rather than derived through exploratory or confirmatory factor analysis. This pattern is consistent with theoretical accounts that conceptualize research competence as embedded within a broader system of methodological, reflective, and professional capacities ( Ivanenko et al., 2015 ; Matjašič and Vogrinc, 2025 ). In the present study, the observed associations suggest that research competence is related to teachers’ social-emotional monitoring practices and readiness to use AI, while the relatively lower baseline score for research competence indicates a potential area for further professional development. The relatively modest baseline scores for research competence further suggest that although many teachers possess a theoretical understanding of educational research, they continue to experience difficulties translating this knowledge into systematic classroom-based inquiry. This interpretation is consistent with the findings reported by Gümüşok et al. (2024) . The second research question focused on teachers’ perceptions of the role of students’ social-emotional well-being in educational research and pedagogical decision-making. The qualitative findings revealed a shift in how participants conceptualized this information following the program. Before participation, teachers tended to describe students’ emotional well-being primarily as a general factor influencing academic achievement and motivation. After the program, participants more frequently emphasized systematic observation, monitoring, and the potential use of social-emotional information as contextual evidence for classroom inquiry and pedagogical decision-making. These findings align with the work of Ng et al. (2025) , who highlighted the importance of social-emotional data for evidence-informed educational decision-making. Similarly, Li and Qian (2025) showed the impact of teacher social-emotional competence on the quality of education. Importantly, the present findings suggest that teachers increasingly recognized the potential of AI to support research-related activities, including the future organization and interpretation of social-emotional information within classroom inquiry. However, the present study did not directly test AI-based analysis of student-level social-emotional data. With respect to the third research question, statistically significant pre–post improvements were observed across all measured constructs following participation in the AI-supported professional development program. The standardized within-participant changes were approximately medium in magnitude (Cohen's d z = 0.47–0.63). The largest standardized pre–post change was observed for teachers’ research competence (d_z = 0.63), which was the primary developmental focus of the program. Given the absence of a comparison group, however, these findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating that the program itself caused the observed improvements. Rather, they indicate that improvements in the measured constructs occurred during the period of program participation. Because AI was embedded within a multicomponent professional development program, the observed changes cannot be attributed specifically to AI. They should instead be interpreted as changes occurring during participation in the integrated program as a whole. The qualitative findings further illustrate the changes in the patterns of teachers’ reported perceptions of AI. Prior to the intervention, AI was predominantly viewed as a tool for searching scientific literature, translating or formatting texts. Following participation in the program, however, teachers increasingly described AI as a methodological partner capable of supporting multiple stages of the research process, including research planning, development of data collection instruments, statistical analysis, interpretation of empirical findings, and evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. These findings are consistent with broader evidence that AI-supported tools can contribute to teachers’ professional activities, although the specific applications examined across previous studies differ from those investigated here. Choi et al. (2023) similarly reported that teachers used an AI chatbot for lesson planning, classroom management, and subject-matter support. The present findings do not demonstrate AI-based analysis of students’ social-emotional data. Rather, they indicate that participants increasingly recognized potential research-related applications of AI. AI-supported analysis of student-level social-emotional data should therefore be regarded as a prospective application of the proposed conceptual framework that requires direct empirical testing. analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. First, the study was conducted with a relatively small sample of 105 in-service chemistry teachers from a single region, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to teachers of other subject areas, educational contexts, or national education systems. Second, the study employed a single-group pre-test/post-test design without a comparison or control group. Consequently, although statistically significant improvements were observed following participation in the professional development program, these changes cannot be attributed exclusively to the program. Alternative explanations, including repeated-measurement effects, maturation, concurrent professional experiences, or other contextual influences during the study period, cannot be ruled out. Future studies employing controlled or quasi-experimental comparative designs are therefore needed to establish whether the observed changes can be specifically attributed to the intervention. Third, the majority of the data were derived from self-report questionnaires and participants’ reflective responses, which may be influenced by social desirability and self-perception biases. Future studies should test these applications directly using ethically collected student-level data and appropriately validated analytical methods. items.abstract_text: Purpose Identifying exceptional leaders remains a top priority for organisations. Traditionally, leaders were selected using a battery of assessments measuring key personal attributes believed to make leaders successful. However, there has been a shift away from selecting leaders based on an a priori list of virtues, towards a focus on the actual behaviours linked to high performance. This abductive approach in competency framework development for leaders starts with the behaviours demonstrated in assessments and then constructs the competency framework in a bottom-up approach. Design/methodology/approach In the current study, a total of 15 411 leaders from 283 different companies and 38 countries completed a 3.5-hour online assessment centre simulation exercise. Natural language processing and machine learning were then utilised to identify 38 competencies by screening more than 30 million words. We then mapped this artificial intelligence-derived framework to prominent leadership models. Findings Despite strong congruence between frameworks, the abductive approach revealed three critical findings: 1) Not all competencies are equally distributed across the leader population; 2) Competencies are distributed across job levels, with some commonly observed in junior leadership roles and others primarily amongst senior leaders; and 3) the artefacts collected by the machine-learning algorithm enable a more granular view of the behaviours that constitute a competency compared to human assessors. Originality/value Using abductive methods to supplement deductive models capitalising on the strengths of both approaches, yield more nuanced leadership competency frameworks.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: East African Journal of Law and Ethics
items.abstract_text: Section 27(5) of Tanzania’s Personal Data Protection Act, Cap 44 R.E. 2023, obliges a data controller to notify the Personal Data Protection Commission ‘without undue delay’ of any security breach affecting personal data, but does not say how long that is, sets no risk threshold for telling the people whose data has been exposed, and is silent on what a controller must do while the facts of an incident are still emerging. The objective of this article is to examine how effectively that duty operates in practice and to identify the lessons that European standards offer for its reform. Adopting an exploratory, qualitative socio-legal design, the study combines a doctrinal reading of the Act and its 2023 Regulations with semi-structured interviews, analysed thematically, with seven purposively selected key informants: four officers of data controller organisations, an official of the Commission, a legal practitioner and a data protection expert. The findings are read against Articles 33 and 34 of the General Data Protection Regulation, Article 7(2) of Convention 108+ and the guidelines of the European Data Protection Board. Organisations follow a consistent but undocumented sequence of technical, legal and management assessment before notifying; every respondent named the undefined timeframe as the main difficulty; direct notification of data subjects is left to case-by-case discretion; and the Commission escalates from guidance to sanction under clear capacity limits. Respondents also warned, independently, against copying the GDPR’s seventy-two-hour rule without the institutional support that makes it workable. The article proposes a defined notification period with phased disclosure, a statutory high-risk threshold for notifying data subjects, scenario-based guidance and published breach statistics, and argues that resourcing the Commission should precede any tighter deadline.

reading.findings: All four respondents from controller organisations described the same staged process: a technical assessment of what happened, a legal or compliance assessment of whether it is notifiable, and a management decision. The compliance officer explained that the organisation first establishes whether personal data has actually been compromised, considering the type of information, the number of people affected and the circumstances, after which the compliance and ICT teams report to management. 40 The ICT manager described the technical team's task as determining whether there had been unauthorised access, loss, alteration or disclosure before passing its findings to the legal team. 41 The legal officer identified the hardest question as telling an internal security incident from a notifiable personal data breach, a distinction the legislation leaves open and which therefore depends on legal 41 Interview with Respondent 2, ICT Manager, data controller organisation (Dar es Salaam, 21 August 2026). advice in each case. 42 The senior manager confirmed that management decides on that advice, weighing the data exposed, the number of people affected and the likely consequences. 43 None of the four described a written risk matrix or methodology. Each spoke of professional judgement exercised case by case. This practice is risk-based in substance but informal in method, and it creates an accountability problem: an organisation that cannot show how it reached a decision will find it hard to defend that decision to the Commission later, even if the decision was right.
reading.interpretation: Tanzania's breach notification regime works in the limited sense that the organisations and the regulator interviewed do investigate incidents, assess them and report them. It falls short of the European benchmark in three related respects: it has no defined notification period and no route for phased reporting, it leaves direct notification of data subjects entirely to the controller's discretion, and it lacks the published guidance and regulatory capacity that make the European rules workable. The evidence from those who apply the law points to the same conclusion as the doctrinal comparison. What Tanzania needs is not the seventy-two-hour figure on its own but the system around it: a period paired with phased disclosure, a clear high-risk threshold for telling the people affected, worked guidance and published statistics, introduced in an order that the Commission can sustain. Borrowing the European rule without that system would repeat the uncertainty it is meant to cure. The evidence reported here comes from seven informants, and it identifies problems rather than measuring their prevalence. Two lines of further research follow. Once the Commission publishes notification statistics, a quantitative study could establish how often, how quickly and by whom breaches are reported across sectors, including the small and micro enterprises that this study's sample did not reach. And a study conducted with the Commission's cooperation, drawing on officials in registration, complaints, investigation and enforcement, could show how notifications are triaged and how the Commission decides when guidance gives way to sanction.

items.abstract_text: ABSTRACT The rapid spread of generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) technologies into various aspects of second/foreign language (L2) education has recently attracted increasing scholarly attention. However, the way GenAI literacy may be associated with English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers' emotional state has received insufficient attention. To address this gap, the present quantitative study drew on control‐value theory (CVT) and the broaden‐and‐build theory (BBT) in examining the role of GenAI literacy and emotional literacy in EFL teachers' teaching enjoyment in the context of AI‐mediated instruction. Three questionnaires were completed by 679 Chinese EFL teachers. The results revealed positive pairwise correlations among GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment.

analysis.methods: A total of 679 Chinese EFL teachers participated in the study. These teachers were recruited via a non-probability purposive sampling procedure. Teachers were eligible to participate if they had experience using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) for teaching or learning purposes. The recruitment pool consisted of the research team's social-media networks and professional contacts, including colleagues working in the field of English-language teaching in China. The recruitment procedure involved voluntary participation; thus, eligible participants were included if they met the inclusion criteria of the study. The inclusion criteria specified that participants should have current or recent teaching experience and prior experience using GenAI for educational purposes. The non-random nature of the sampling procedure should be taken into account when interpreting the results; accordingly, one should speak of applicability to the sampled population of Chinese EFL teachers, rather than generalizability to the population of Chinese EFL teachers. The teachers who participated in the study were relatively experienced in teaching English: their ages ranged from 30 to 55, and all the participants had at least 5 years of teaching experience. Of the 679 teachers, 185 (27%) were male and 494 (73%) were female. In terms of the participants' academic backgrounds, 211 (31%) had a master's degree and 468 (69%) had a doctoral degree, mostly in English-related disciplines. Concerning the teachers' English-language proficiency, 263 (39%) participants were upper-intermediate and 416 (61%) were advanced English learners and users. These characteristics indicate that the sample was rather high-status and experienced in terms of teaching English. Therefore, the results should not be generalized to Chinese EFL teachers who are younger, less qualified or less experienced. Additional demographic and professional characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 1 . This study employed a quantitative research design to examine the relationships among Chinese EFL teachers' GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment in the context of AI-mediated education. Data were collected through an online questionnaire administered via Wenjuanxing. A link to the online questionnaire was shared with EFL teachers through social media and professional contacts. Because all participants reported at least upper-intermediate English proficiency, the questionnaires were administered in English. The questionnaire comprised 72 scale items across the three instruments. Before completing the questionnaire, participants were informed of the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation and the confidentiality of their responses and informed consent was obtained from all participants. All responses were collected and processed anonymously, and participants were informed that they could withdraw from the study at any time. Data collection lasted approximately 1 month, yielding 679 valid responses for subsequent analysis. The collected responses were then checked for accuracy and entered into an Excel file before the final statistical analysis.
analysis.discussion: This study aimed to examine the associations among GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment of Chinese EFL teachers. The study revealed that both constructs of GenAI literacy and emotional literacy had a significant and positive correlation with teaching enjoyment, which is theoretically supported by BBT in the sense that positive emotions, behaviours and repertoires usually trigger other positive feelings and outcomes (Fredrickson 2001) . The association between GenAI literacy and teaching enjoyment advances prior research, which has mostly focused on the measurement of GenAI and its ecological factors (e.g., Wang et al. 2025; Yang and Derakhshan 2026) . In other words, the emotional aspect of GenAI literacy is what makes this research different from the literature. Likewise, Seyri and Ghiasvand (2025) reported that EFL teachers, who used GenAI tools during writing instruction experienced teaching enjoyment while using GenAI tools in writing instruction. It can also be postulated that high GenAI literacy could be accompanied by high teaching enjoyment in teachers in light of their positive appraisals of AI adoption and their control over such technologies. This justification aligns with CVT of emotions as well (Pekrun 2006 ). The engaging nature of AI tools may further explain why teachers with higher GenAI literacy reported more teaching enjoyment. Another finding in this study was that emotional literacy correlated positively with teaching enjoyment. The emotional components of emotional literacy (e.g., motivation, emotional awareness, empathy and self-regulation) may have fostered its interplay with enjoyment, which is per se an emotion. In simple terms, the emotional essence of these two constructs may justify the obtained result in this study, a claim resonating with the conceptualizations of FLTE (Proietti Ergün and Dewaele 2021). The interconnection between EFL teachers' emotional literacy and other positive psycho-affective factors is empirically supported by Yang et al. (2025) as well. Another explanation for this outcome can be the role of emotional literacy in teachers' professionalism as a whole. The emotional nature of L2 teaching may offer another explanation (Her and De Costa 2022) . The demands of the AI age for being literate in various aspects further clarify the study. The study also indicated that both GenAI literacy and emotional literacy were each positively associated with EFL teachers' teaching enjoyment when modelled simultaneously. Given the cross-sectional design, the direction of these associations cannot be established; reverse or reciprocal relations (e.g., teachers who enjoy teaching may invest more in developing their literacies) are equally plausible. This might be because higher GenAI literacy may be associated with greater perceived competence and confidence in using AI tools. High GenAI literacy may also turn AI technologies into assistants and resources rather than threats. Hence, teachers enjoy such integration more. Emotional literacy may have been associated with teaching enjoyment because teachers with high emotional literacy are able to detect and regulate their own and others' emotions. This emotional regulation competency is more essential in unfamiliar and new contexts like AI-mediated education. Emotional literacy may also serve as a protector of teachers' positive emotions and support deeper engagement in their work despite inherent challenges. Another possible explanation for this finding can be the idea that teachers' emotional literacy lays the groundwork for a better classroom rapport with students, who actively participate in activities and interactions. Therefore, teachers are more likely to enjoy their job. The study extends the literature on GenAI literacy by positing that GenAI literacy does not operate in emotion-free or emotionally neutral zones. Technically, it highlights an emotional dimension in the ecological system of GenAI literacy (see Yang and Derakhshan 2026) . As tenable by CVT, the participants' positive view of AI technologies and their ability to effectively use them in L2 classes may be the root of experiencing high GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment (Pekrun 2006) . The overall landscape of AI-mediated L2 education is claimed to be emotional and contingent on teachers' technical literacy, as empirically noted in the literature (Alrabai and Derakhshan 2026; Wang et al. 2025) . This quantitative study examined the associations among GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and EFL teachers' general teaching enjoyment among teachers with prior GenAI-use experience. The study concludes that teachers' GenAI literacy is not confined to technical aspects but is positively associated with teaching enjoyment as well. Based on the results, teachers' general teaching enjoyment is positively associated with their GenAI literacy and emotional literacy among teachers with prior GenAI-use experience. The simultaneous emphasis on GenAI and emotional literacies in this study further reflects the complexities of the AI age and the expectations from teachers to be competent and literate in various aspects. The findings are broadly consistent with CVT and BBT, which were used as post hoc interpretive lenses for the observed associations. However, the proposed mechanisms involving control appraisals and the broadening of positive emotions were not directly measured or tested in this study. Accordingly, the findings may inform the application of these theories to AI-mediated L2 education but should not be interpreted as a direct test or extension of either theory. Practically, EFL teachers may find the study valuable for understanding the emotional consequences of AI-mediated L2 education. Their attitudes towards AI technologies may also change to positive in light of their academic and emotional outcomes. Teachers can engage in self and other-directed professional development courses related to AI and PP to be equipped with required literacies of the AI age. Their attitudes towards AI technologies may also change to positive in light of their academic and emotional outcomes. Teacher educators can use this study as a guide to design and provide multi-session workshops and seminars for novice and experienced EFL teachers teaching them how to regulate AI-induced emotions and practically develop their GenAI and emotional literacies. Trainers can engage teachers in activities and scenarios in which they need to react to an emotional situation in AI-mediated L2 classes. The emotional aspects of AI-mediated education can be equally focused upon in teacher professional development programs. Currently, most such programs are limited to pedagogical aspects and implications of AI integration. Policymakers may find the findings insightful for revisiting their plans and decisions regarding technical supports, AI infrastructures and budget to provide EFL teachers with premium packages of AI tools that foster their AI literacy and efficacy. Teacher-education curricula may incorporate the emotional dimensions of GenAI integration alongside technical and pedagogical training. GenAI tools designers and companies may draw on this study to focus more on the emotional outcomes of their proposed tools. The emotional sensitivity and responsiveness of their tools may be updated in the future.
analysis.limitations: Despite its contributions, the study contained some limitations that trigger future studies. First, the use of a pure quantitative design limits the insights to numerical values without depth. Future qualitative studies using interviews and observations may add meaning and depth to the quantitative outcomes. Second, the use of purposive sampling may endanger the representativeness of the sample. It is interesting to collect diverse data from diverse locations using probability-based or stratified multisite sampling in the future. Third, drawing on one-shot surveys limits the credibility and rigour of the study. Future researchers are recommended to take a triangulated approach using several instruments. The longitudinal nature of GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment was overlooked in this research. So, scholars are suggested to run longitudinal and multi-phase studies that analyse data on a time-series basis. The study only explored statistical associations among the constructs without seeking the underlying reasons behind their correlation. Hence, it is a good idea to add a semi-structured interview asking the participants to elaborate on the reasons and mechanisms through which the three variables of the study interact. The study was limited to the EFL context of China. So, cross-cultural studies are recommendable as teachers with diverse backgrounds may have different perspectives of the interplay of GenAI and emotional literacies with teaching enjoyment. Researchers are also advised to develop universal models/frameworks for AI-mediated L2 education with special attention to the emotional aspects of this mode of instruction. In addition, all constructs were measured by self-report in a single questionnaire, so common method variance may have inflated the associations and teaching enjoyment was measured in general rather than specifically for AI-mediated teaching, which limits conclusions about enjoyment in AI-mediated instruction.

items.abstract_text: Background The global proliferation of generative artificial intelligence has transformed safety governance into a highly contested sociopolitical battleground, yet existing discourse studies frequently under-theorize the micro-cognitive mechanisms of epistemic reality construction within AI safety standardization. Objective To investigate how corporate and regulatory actors engineer divergent cognitive realities of AI safety through specific micro-grammatical choices. Methods We proposed an integrated Cognitive-Critical Discourse Analysis framework by synthesizing Langacker's cognitive conception of reality with Fairclough's three-dimensional model, and applied it to a comparative corpus of corporate safety frameworks and regulatory policy documents. Results Tech enterprises engineer a reality of techno-pragmatic containment via active voice, high-certainty evidentiality, and immediate projection to naturalize self-regulation. Conversely, regulatory bodies construct a reality of socio-structural vulnerability using distal modals, passive constructions, and deontic mandates to legitimize state-enforced compliance. Conclusions Linguistic normalization is actively deployed to facilitate or contest corporate epistemic hegemony in AI governance. These findings provide empirical references for revising regulatory discourse and enhancing public media literacy against algorithmic exceptionalism.

Consequently, we constructed a specialized comparative corpus representing the two dominant institutional factions: regulatory authorities (supranational entities and sovereign states) and regulated entities (leading technology corporations holding market monopolies). At the macro-level of data collection, representative and authoritative texts were assembled to ensure comprehensive coverage. The regulatory sub-corpus (Corpus B) comprises macro-policy frameworks, notably the U.S. Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, the OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence, and Singapore's Model AI Governance Framework and so on. Conversely, the corporate sub-corpus (Corpus A) encompasses technical standards and safety frameworks from industry leaders, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Huawei and so on. Collectively, these carefully clipped texts constitute a targeted, domain-specific corpus of contemporary institutional AI safety discourse, offering a focused empirical basis for analyzing the discursive tension between political regulation and technological capital. To mitigate the inherent genre asymmetry between the macrosocietal focus of regulatory policy documents and the highly technical, engineering-centric nature of corporate manuals, a rigorous, protocol-driven thematic clipping strategy was operationalized. Rather than conducting a crude full-text comparison, which would inevitably skew the statistical data toward irrelevant technical jargon in Corpus A, the compilation process employed a targeted extraction protocol. Specifically, the tables of contents and structural headers of all corporate documents were systematically screened to isolate core chapters directly addressing risk mitigation mechanisms, responsibility demarcations, and safety compliance protocols. To strictly operationalize this thematic clipping and guarantee that no relevant discursive information was inadvertently missed, the excluded technical sections (e.g., mathematical proofs, computational benchmarking, and software code snippets) underwent a secondary validation protocol. This involved automated concordancing with a predefined lexical set of governance-related keywords (e.g., safety, ethics, risk, compliance, liability), which empirically confirmed the total absence of epistemic or regulatory claims within the omitted structural data. Because this study investigates the linguistic construction of safety governance as a sociopolitical phenomenon rather than the mathematical validity of the AI models, the exclusion of purely computational segments is theoretically justified. This rigorous thematic alignment maximizes functional and semantic parity between the opposing camps and eliminates structural noise without compromising the integrity of the critical discourse analysis. Following these procedures, the finalized bipartite corpus yielded highly balanced datasets (see Table 1 ), with Corpus A totaling 116,082 tokens and Corpus B reaching 116,636 tokens, thereby securing a robust quantitative baseline for subsequent analysis.

While the literature documents benefits in operational efficiency and decision quality, most concrete evidence focuses primarily on internal efficiency. Urban digital twins have become commonplace in most European cities and smart cities globally. However, the role of AI within urban digital twins remains comparatively underexplored. This article addresses these gaps through a qualitative analysis of AI in Helsinki’s Experimentation Accelerator platform experiments and by comparing them against a DT framework based on the literature. Through this, we analyze how AI is piloted in municipal applications and how the identified use cases of AI align with the components of urban digital twins, identifying potential roles for AI in the urban digital twin as well as directions for future development.

These core relationships remained stable after controlling for students’ background characteristics and initial levels. Classroom engagement, flow experience, and musical emotional intelligence all showed significant positive developmental trends across the five measurement occasions. In the unconditional growth models, the mean slopes of the three variables were all significantly greater than zero, and the slope variances were all significant. Thus, within the learning period covered by this study, the three variables not only changed overall but also differed noticeably in their pace of development across students. Compared with level differences at a single time point, these growth trajectories more directly capture how students change over sustained learning. The growth in classroom engagement indicates that students’ investment in classroom tasks is not a fixed state but adjusts with ongoing learning experiences. As students become more familiar with task formats and classroom expectations, their ways of participating may also stabilize. Flow experience showed a similar developmental pattern. Sustained learning gives students opportunities to continually adjust the match between their abilities and task demands and to form more stable attention investment and activity absorption. The growth in musical emotional intelligence reflects that emotional abilities themselves have room for development. Music learning continuously involves perceiving emotional information in music and regulating one’s own emotional states, and these experiences accumulate through repeated practice. Musical emotional intelligence is therefore not merely a stable characteristic students have already formed before entering the classroom. The significant slope variance of all three variables also deserves attention. An overall average increase does not mean that all students follow the same developmental pattern. Some students improved relatively quickly during the study, while others changed more modestly. The parallel-process growth model builds on such individual differences in development to further examine whether different processes of change are interrelated. This study therefore asks whether a student’s speed of change in one psychological process is related to their speed of change in another psychological process. The positive relationship between growth in classroom engagement and growth in flow experience supported H1. In the three-process model, the classroom engagement slope was significantly positively correlated with the flow slope. In the growth mediation model, the path between engagement growth and flow growth also remained significant. Compared with the relationship whereby students with higher engagement at a given time point also have higher flow, this study reveals a connection between two psychological processes in terms of their rates of change. Students whose classroom engagement grew faster also tended to show faster growth in flow experience. Classroom engagement and flow represent different aspects of learning, and their linked growth suggests that sustained participation may provide more opportunities for concentration and task absorption. A higher level of engagement does not necessarily produce flow, but sustained increases in engagement can increase students’ opportunities to engage with tasks, process feedback, and adjust their performance. When students can invest more stably in the current task, the conditions needed to maintain attention and form activity absorption also increase. The relationship between classroom engagement and flow is therefore evident not only in level differences but also in its clear developmental properties. The significant relationship between growth in flow experience and growth in musical emotional intelligence supported H2. In the three-process model, the two slopes were significantly positively correlated, and in the growth mediation model, the path between flow growth and musical emotional intelligence growth was likewise significant. One important feature that distinguishes music learning from general knowledge learning is that the learning process itself continuously involves emotional information. When performing, listening, or composing, students not only need to complete tasks but also need to perceive musical expression and continually adjust their own emotional states. The sustained attention and deep absorption of flow allow learners to maintain processing of such information for extended periods. As deep immersive experience strengthens over the course of learning, processing experiences related to musical emotions may also accumulate in parallel. The key point here is not that flow itself equals musical emotional intelligence, but that the developmental processes of the two are systematically connected. Repeated experiences of flow during music learning may provide opportunities for students to recognize and regulate their emotions during practice and performance. This study therefore advances the relationship between flow and musical emotional intelligence from psychological covariation at a single time point to a connection between rates of development. items.title: Mapping Women’s Contributions to Artificial Intelligence Using Large-Scale Text Analysis

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Participation in AI research shapes which type of AI is built, whose societal needs it addresses, and how it is used in society. Despite increasing attention to gender diversity in AI, we lack systematic evidence on the research topics, methods used, and collaboration structures associated with female AI researchers. This paper addresses this significant gap by developing the first large-scale, validated mapping of women’s contributions to both generative and non-generative AI research across data science and the main social science disciplines (economics, political science, and sociology). Using a sample of over 500,000 papers published between 2023 and 2026, we document three key findings. First, women are under-represented among academic AI authors across all four disciplines and recent years, and least represented in data science. Second, conditional on participating, women’s AI research is thematically distinctive: it is more applied, social and purpose-driven, concentrated in health, education and fairness, and, in data science, oriented towards using rather than building AI. Third, this distinctive work is heard less: conditional on working on the same AI topic women and men are cited equally, but the topics women disproportionately work on are themselves cited less, so women’s ideas receive systematically fewer citations. This voice gap is therefore a topic-composition penalty rather than a same-topic penalty, and it reduces efficiency by giving a distinctive, society-oriented research agenda too little voice in how AI develops.

items.title: Overcoming Dengue Underreporting: A Machine Learning Framework for Automated Dengue Notification Based on Electronic Medical Records

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Hospital notification of dengue cases is frequently delayed, contributing to underreporting. At Thai provincial hospitals the bottleneck is administrative, not diagnostic: delayed discharge coding and clerical steps mean notifications are submitted late or omitted. Existing machine learning (ML) studies require clinician-annotated features absent in passive electronic medical records (EMRs). We propose a dual-pathway EMR framework for ML-based pre-population of surveillance reports. We analyzed 1031 dengue-suspected encounters (508 notifiable) from Surin Hospital, Thailand (2019–2022). Pathway A combines EMR data with manually documented clinical features; Pathway B uses only passive EMR data. Using an 80/20 stratified split, we tested 7 ML methods across 11 feature sets (77 combinations) with SHAP-guided feature elimination and 10-fold cross-validation. On the primary split, Pathway A (CatBoost) achieved an F1 score of 96.62%, 95.10% sensitivity, and 98.10% specificity (10-seed mean F1 95.7% ± 1.4%). Pathway B (LightGBM) achieved an F1 score of 84.42%, 94.12% sensitivity, 75.24% specificity, and a projected negative predictive value of 99.1% at 10% prevalence; 10-seed performance was lower (F1 78.5% ± 4.3%; sensitivity 89.1%). An exploratory LSTM-16 stacking model (F1 83.99%; precision 79.49%) performed best in precision and specificity among Pathway B. Test F1 SD across 10 seeds was ≤5.0% in 75 of 77 combinations. Within this cohort, passive EMR modeling achieved 91–94% sensitivity on the primary split (85–89% across seeds) without additional data collection, supporting the feasibility of ML-based notification in resource-constrained hospitals. Whether this reduces dengue underreporting must be established in prospective, multi-center studies.

At the same time, with the improvement of natural language processing, big data analysis, and platform intelligent services, the positioning of AI chatbots in cus- tomer service is also gradually transforming from auxiliary tools into core service carriers. Therefore, this study aims to focus on AI chatbots on Meituan’s instant retail platform, explore the actual user experience of Genera- tion Z, and propose corresponding user experience enhancement strategies. In terms of research results, the conclusions of this study show some consistency with existing research. First, existing research suggests that the user experience of AI chatbots is primarily influenced by factors such as inter- action quality, emotional perception, privacy transparency, and personalized services74,75. Although this study focuses on Generation Z, it likewise found that users’ demands for Meituan AI chatbots are mainly concentrated on aspects such as how to provide more effective interaction experiences, personalized online services, and service assurance. Among them, the needs with relatively high importance weights are ranked in order as smart interactive experience (0.5915) and personalized experience (0.2069), which also reflects that, compared with the experience influencing factors of other dimensions, Generation Z pays more attention to relying on AI chatbots to more quickly resolve their own usage demands and improve the personalized interaction and anthropomorphic level in the interaction process. Second, existing research points out that dialogue tone, emotional responses, and interface friendliness can improve user satisfaction and sense of participation34,35,76. This is also relatively consis- tent with the findings of this study. According to the AHP weight analysis results, requirement types such as quick access to feature, humanized AI interaction, personalized avatars for AI chatbots, and interface design optimiza- tion had relatively high weight values. At the same time, the requirement weights of intelligent emotion-aware interaction, AI personalized recommendation, and smart content recommendation were also relatively high. This indicates that Generation Z users’ actual experiences with AI chatbots may be related to dimensions such as emo- tional interaction and personalized services. In addition, existing studies have suggested that privacy statements and user trust may affect user satisfaction. In this study, privacy transparency was classified as one-dimensional quality in the KANO model evaluation, while the AHP weight analysis also showed that service trust and assur- ance needs was one of the important requirements. This result is relatively consistent with existing studies, indi- cating that information transparency and user trust are important factors in the user experience of AI chatbots. Compared to existing research, this study has also yielded new findings in its conclusions. Existing research suggests that AI chatbots can effectively enhance satisfaction and user experience by providing instant responses, accurately addressing user needs, and improving service quality. However, this study found that Generation Z is more concerned with achieving interaction efficiency, validity, and satisfaction during the process of using AI chatbots. Second, in existing research, factors such as semantic understanding, context awareness, and dialogue tone are considered to influence the user experience of AI chatbots. The research results indicate that Generation Z users’ needs for AI chatbots are not solely concentrated on the language interaction capabilities of AI chatbots, but rather present the combined influence of basic functional assurance, service experience optimization, and added value. Third, existing research suggests that personalized services help improve user experience and satis- faction. This study also found that Generation Z users’ demand for personalization is more focused on the experi- ential aspect. In the AHP weighting results, personalized AI chatbot avatar ranked 3rd, humanized AI interaction ranked 2nd, and interface design optimization ranked 4th, while smart content recommendation ranked 10th and AI personalized recommendation ranked 7th. From this, it can be seen that Generation Z’s needs for personalized services are not only personalized recommendations or service content, but are gradually expanding to experien- tial aspects such as AI chatbot avatar, emotional interaction, and interface styles. This study has the following theoretical values and practical significance. First, through empirical research, this study classified, screened, and ranked the experience pain points and further experience needs of Generation Z users when using AI chatbots on instant retail platforms. This helps to understand the actual experiences of Generation Z users with AI chatbots, thereby providing empirical evidence for constructing a theoretical system of user experience for AI chatbots on instant retail platforms. According to the research results, this study found that even for AI chatbots, it is still necessary to provide quick access to feature, which helps improve the conve- nience and effectiveness of interaction. In addition, Generation Z users also attached relatively high importance to experience factors such as humanized AI interaction and personalized avatars for AI chatbots. These experi- ence needs have rarely been mentioned in previous studies. These new findings can provide new evidence for the subsequent construction of a theoretical system of AI chatbot user experience. Second, previous user experience studies have focused more on user experience issues related to interface touch interaction and physical interac- tion. This study further extends the research object to the exploration of interaction behaviors between humans and intelligent agents, which can further enrich the user experience perspective in the field of human–computer interaction and supplement empirical research on user experience between humans and intelligent agents. In addition, it can also supplement empirical findings on the user experience of Generation Z users when using AI chatbots on instant retail platforms. items.abstract_text: Abstract Objective To better understand how physicians view the potential use of artificial intelligence (AI) in their practices. Method We conducted an online cross-sectional survey of 1,258 physicians (MD, DO, MBBS or equivalent) in the United States (US) and Canada from December 2023 through February 2026. The survey contained 34 questions focused on 6 areas: (1) demographics, (2) training, (3) clinical benefits, (4) clinical concerns, (5) clinical AI prediction tools, and (6) generative AI. Results A total of 130 completed surveys were received (response rate, 10%). Top specialties included psychiatry (46.2%), internal medicine (14.6%) and pediatrics (13.8%). A total of 16.9% had training in computer science or information technology and 40.8% in statistics. Nearly half (46.9%) had no formal training in AI and were self-taught. Those with training in AI received it through vendors or at work. Sixty to seventy percent thought AI would provide diagnostic aid or treatment recommendations, but half did not feel adequately trained to safely use AI in practice. Over 70% thought it could help with administrative tasks. More than 80% were worried about errors, misinformation, or biases in the data. Conclusion There is a growing sense that AI in medicine could be helpful with specific tasks. Ongoing training, education, and study are needed to determine how AI will best integrate into clinical practice. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly being marketed for and integrated into clinical medicine. Previous physician surveys have shown that physicians are optimistic, yet cautious, about its implementation. This study utilizes a novel survey tool to assess physician attitudes toward the integration of AI in practice, highlighting the desire for ongoing education around and monitoring of AI among physicians in the United States and Canada. There is a growing recognition that AI, while a powerful tool, may harbor biases, promulgate misinformation, and lead to harm to patients, and requires ongoing training and oversight by humans.

items.abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support reasoning and decision-making, raising questions about how AI influences reflective cognition and trust. This study examined how AI pedigree and reliability influenced cognitive reflection performance, cognitive load, trust, and performance overestimation during a verbal Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT-V). Participants ( N = 148) were assigned to a no-AI control condition, a low-pedigree AI condition, or a high-pedigree AI condition. Participants in the high-pedigree AI condition demonstrated significantly greater trust and CRT performance than participants in both other conditions while also exhibiting lower performance overestimation. AI access did not significantly reduce perceived cognitive load, although greater cognitive load predicted poorer CRT performance overall. Importantly, trust interacted with AI condition such that greater trust predicted lower CRT performance in the low-pedigree AI condition but not in the high-pedigree AI condition. These findings support theories of calibrated reliance rather than indiscriminate cognitive offloading.

items.abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is vital to healthcare system transformation. Existing research mainly focuses on the macro-level technological empowerment of AI, yet insufficiently explores how healthcare organizations’ strategic commitment to AI translates into better medical service outcomes through individual psychological mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach From the perspective of human-AI collaboration, we utilize survey data collected from medical staff working in Chinese medical institutions to examine the mediating mechanisms and boundary conditions linking organizational AI orientation and AI value co-creation outcomes. Findings Drawing on social cognitive theory, the results reveal that healthcare organizations’ AI orientation is positively related to medical staff’s AI value co-creation outcomes, and AI self-efficacy mediates this relationship. Moreover, their creative self-efficacy positively moderates the relationship between AI self-efficacy and AI value co-creation. Originality/value This study clarifies the micro-level transmission paths between organizational AI orientation and medical staff’s value co-creation outcomes. It provides new insights for hospitals to enhance medical service quality and optimize human-AI collaboration during AI-driven healthcare organizational transformation.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the environment of language learning, but its theoretical basis and ethical boundaries have not been fully explored. This paper builds a multi-level analytical system for AI-assisted language learning based on cognitive load theory, the zone of proximal development, generative linguistics and the technology acceptance model. AI can help students learn better by reducing extraneous cognitive load and providing easy-to-access support and instant correction; however, due to technological limitations, it may also reduce students' sense of ability and self-management. Generative linguistics and generative AI are not in opposition; rather, the former advocates for data frugality and innate mechanisms, while the latter is characterized by data maximalism and statistical learning; they are in harmony at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program. According to the above research, chatbots have shown a modest positive effect on language learning; this degree varies depending on the learner's level, interface Design, interaction characteristics, etc. Based on the above, this paper introduces a "Smart Chinese" collaborative learning plugin that integrates ChatGPT with special scaffolding tools for assessment, planning, practice, feedback and community support. Finally, it presents the ethical problems of algorithmic bias, data privacy, over-reliance, and educational gaps, and proposes a multi-level governance system at the institutional, technological and pedagogical levels.

reading.findings: Recently, there have been many studies abroad on artificial intelligence-aided language learning. A meta-analysis of the 28 studies and 70 effect sizes found that chatbot-assisted language learning has a moderate positive effect compared with non-chatbot conditions, and this effect is moderated by educational level, language proficiency, interface design and interactional capability [1] . Therefore, AI cannot achieve good results on its own; it is only effective when matched with suitable teaching plans and students. Natural language processing tools can be used to conduct interactive and personalised exercises for learning specialised vocabulary. A case study showed that the learners' understanding of sustainability-related vocabulary increased significantly, and they could use the new words in context [11] . In pronunciation training, a speech-based ChatGPT intervention showed that learners continuously improved in multiple recordings and maintained the gains in a delayed posttest; thus, AI interaction can promote both immediate performance and long-term learning [12] . AI-simulated interlocutors in interactional competence can generate preferred responses, repair strategies and culturally appropriate closing remarks, but different models vary in the clarity and pragmatism of scaffolding [13] . Additionally, the impact of AI-generated stories and gamified learning on vocabulary retention and engagement has also been studied [14] . Together, these studies indicate that the effectiveness of AI is related to task authenticity, high-quality feedback and deep learner involvement.
reading.interpretation: In this paper, the five directions of research for generative AI-assisted language learning are: cognitive mechanisms, theoretical contradictions, empirical evidence, application design and ethical governance. According to the study, the main goal of artificial intelligence in education is not to substitute teachers but to enlarge the scope of language learning by reducing students' extraneous cognitive load, providing on-demand scaffolding, generating contextualized materials and offering timely feedback. The conflict between generative linguistics and generative AI is not absolute; rather, at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program, the two are in harmony. Based on the above empirical research, chatbots have provided some help for language learning, but this advantage varies according to the level of study and the design of interaction. Based on the above analysis, this paper puts forward a "Smart Chinese" collaborative learning plugin that integrates ChatGPT with special scaffolding tools to build a closed-loop system of assessment, planning, practice, feedback, updating and community support. Finally, this paper presents some ethical problems of AI language education, such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, over-reliance and educational disparity, and proposes a multi-stakeholder governance system to address these issues. Future research can explore the long-term effects of AI on minority and marginalized languages, pragmatics, cultural adaptation, and thus move from "instrumental assistance" to "ecological integration".

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: WORK: A Journal of Prevention, Assessment & Rehabilitation
items.abstract_text: Background Occupational therapists working in cognitive rehabilitation may face high cognitive demands, and professional isolation. Although AI is used for information retrieval and decision support, its role in supporting reflective clinical reasoning remains insufficiently conceptualized. As scholarly attention shifts from automation toward augmentation of professional judgment, the next step is to understand how AI may support reflective reasoning in complex rehabilitation work. Objective To examine key challenges in cognitive rehabilitation and explore how these needs may inform a conceptual design for GenAI-mediated mentoring within clinical work. Methods A qualitative study grounded in Design Thinking methodology was conducted with 30 female occupational therapists (age range 24–64 years, M = 41.26, SD = 10.35) with wide range of clinical experience (less than one year to more than 20 years) from diverse settings. They completed a demographic questionnaire and participated in two Design Thinking workshops (n = 14; n = 16). Seven participants subsequently engaged in follow-up interviews to refine design implications. All sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed thematically. Results The thematic analysis yielded four themes: (A) The Therapist's role (B) Challenging therapist-client interactions, (C) Loneliness of the Therapist (D) Expectations for guidance or support aspects. These findings informed the conceptualization of a GenAI mentoring framework grounded in real-world clinical demands. Conclusions The findings support the design of generative AI systems as dialogic, context-sensitive tools intended to strengthen professional judgment, warranting further examination of their integration within real-world clinical workflows.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may help students produce higher-quality work; however, its effects on their future ability to work independently remain unclear. This integrative review examines this distinction by analysing research on feedback, metacognitive monitoring, cognitive offloading, and reconstructive learning activities. Targeted web searches and primary-source tracing informed a focused synthesis of adult learning studies and relevant foundational research. Three features may help explain variation in findings across studies: the information feedback conveys, the reasoning learners are expected to undertake and demonstrate, and the conditions under which learning is assessed. The proposed framework distinguishes between a regulatory pathway, in which feedback informs judgments and learning choices, and a practice pathway, in which reconstruction prompts relevant reasoning. This distinction helps explain why learners may become better calibrated without learning more, or learn more without becoming better calibrated. Feedback is expected to enhance the benefits of reconstruction when it improves engagement or reasoning quality, although its incremental benefit may be limited when the activity already provides comparable practice. Four conditional propositions describe these relationships and suggest comparisons that could help distinguish them from the effects of additional instruction, exposure, time, and motivation. The framework provides a foundation for testing when feedback and reconstruction support performance in the absence of assistance. The available evidence is not yet sufficient to establish the full causal pathways or lasting changes in capability, underscoring the value of delayed assessments, transfer tasks, and longitudinal research.

To interpret either result meaningfully, describe the intervention, learner activity, and assessment criterion. This approach also gives mixed ﬁndings a clear er and more substantive role in theory development. The beneﬁts of structur ed tutoring challenge explanations that treat AI assistance solely as a substitute for learners’ cognitive work, while the beneﬁts of continuous access pr ompt reconsideration of the assumption that restrictions are invariably protective. The selected evidence does not establish calibration as a necessary mediator of learning beneﬁts; the pr ecision, timing and coverage of monitoring measures also limit this inference. An experimentally time-matched comparison is needed to determine whether reconstruction offers beneﬁts be yond additional learning time. A useful theory should accommodate these comparisons by specifying conditions in advance, thereby allowing the evidence to inform its predictions meaningfully. The theoretical contribution offers a conditional explanation of when information about learning can be used in practice. The framework distinguishes among diﬃculties in interpr eting feedback, acting on information once it is understood, and developing accurate, relevant reasoning. These challenges can lead to similar overall outcomes, but each may call for a different instructional response. More feedback may be insuﬃcient when learners lack a workable str ategy, and more demanding activities may be ineffective if they reinforce inaccurate reasoning. This distinction also helps explain why improved calibration does not always lead to better learning. The explanation remains provisional: it would be less convincing if distinguishing feedback information from reconstruction requirements added little explanatory value beyond differences in instructional content, exposure, time, or motivation. In educational practice, it helps to start by identifying the intended learning outcome. An activity may be designed to improve work completed with assistance, develop independent skills, or achieve both objectives. Students beneﬁt fr om understanding this goal, and tasks should provide opportunities to practise and demonstrate the relevant skills. A single set of access restrictions is unlikely to be appropriate for all learners. A learner still developing prerequisite knowledge may beneﬁt fr om an explanation before attempting a problem, while another may be ready to develop and defend a solution independently. When aligned with the learning objective, brief unaided assessments and focused reconstruction can help demonstrate progress, with support tailored to the task and the learner. Feedback is most valuable when grounded in available evidence. A recorded action can document how AI was used, while a test score can indicate performance on the assessed tasks. Neither, on its own, supports a broad judgment about a student’s cognitive dependence. Reconstruction can make a student’s reasoning easier to evaluate, but it is useful only when the resulting work is relevant and accurate. Novices may also beneﬁt fr om examples or continued access to sources as they work. These considerations favour learning activities with clear, observable purposes and access arrangements 9.3 Limitations and Further Research The review has several limitations related to its search and selection processes. Web-based searches tend to favor sources that are readily accessible and well indexed. In contrast, the selected search terms and the focus on English-language publications may have excluded relevant work described using different terminology or published in other languages. The focus on text-generating systems also limits the ﬁndings' applicability t o other modalities. Some recent results remain provisional, and for several peripheral sources, claims relied on primary abstracts or publication records because information was limited. The review did not include comprehensive database coverage, duplicate screening, or a formal risk-of-bias assessment. Accordingly, the synthesis presents a focused conceptual argument, while the completeness and balance of the underlying sources remain uncertain. This framework focuses on adult learning contexts in which learners are expected to perform independently of AI at a later stage. Much of the educational evidence reviewed is drawn from university students completing short, structured tasks; therefore, further research is needed to assess its applicability to experienced professionals, workplace learning, other languages, and sustained AI use (Simons et al., 2017). In these contexts, prior knowledge, incentives, and the consequences of errors may inﬂuence how f eedback and reconstruction function. items.title: EVALUATING THE ACCURACY AND RELIABILITY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CHATBOTS IN ANSWERING DENTAL SPECIALTY EXAMINATION PERIODONTOLOGY QUESTIONS

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background/Aim: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly utilized by dental students and specialty candidates as supplementary tools for examination preparation. However, their reliability in specialized clinical domains requiring analytical reasoning remains underexplored. This study aimed to comparatively evaluate the accuracy, reliability, and inter-model agreement of three contemporary reasoning-focused LLMs in answering Periodontology questions from the Turkish Dental Specialty Examination (DUS).Materials and Methods: In this cross-sectional in silico study, 100 multiple-choice Periodontology questions administered in past DUS sessions (2012–2026) were selected. The questions were presented in isolated sessions without prior contextual prompting to three models: OpenAI GPT-5.5 Thinking, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 (adaptive thinking), and Google Gemini 3.1 Pro. Responses were scored dichotomously against official answer keys. Overall accuracy rates were compared using Cochran's Q test, pairwise agreement was assessed via Cohen's Kappa (k) coefficient, and shared error distributions were analyzed using a two-tailed Binomial test (p 0.05), ChatGPT and Gemini selected the identical incorrect distractor in all 5 questions they mutually failed (100% shared error rate; p = 0.0625).Conclusion: Contemporary reasoning-capable LLMs demonstrate high accuracy and substantial inter-model consistency on specialty-level Periodontology questions. Nevertheless, the presence of concordant errors indicates shared algorithmic blind spots, underscoring that AI outputs must be supplemented by specialist oversight and evidence-based verification in dental education.

items.abstract_text: AI-assisted systems redistribute cognitive work before final decisions are made, yet broad labels such as assistance, automation, and human involvement do not fully describe these arrangements. This theory-led structured narrative review connects Function Allocation with research on complementarity, appropriate reliance, cognitive offloading, delegation, mixed initiative, agency, and recovery. It draws on concept-driven retrieval, citation chaining, and selected theoretical foundations. Source selection and coding were AI-assisted, with verification boundaries reported separately. Framework A is a configuration-oriented integrative reporting framework and design space organized around allocation object, performer, allocation authority, change dynamics, and recovery architecture. Framework B provides a conditional temporal process lens on enactment, monitoring, recovery, and reallocation. Together, they support comparison of configuration descriptions across heterogeneous studies while separating configuration, operating conditions, process, and outcomes. The five dimensions build on established constructs. Coding reproducibility, comparative usefulness, and effects on interface design have not been empirically established.

items.title: Exhibiting AI images: Unexpected outputs, linguistic inequalities, and curatorial possibilities

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Structured around latent data spaces that store masses of semantic associations, AI image generators have an intrinsic capacity to draw connections their users might not expect. Their outputs thus have the potential to engender characteristically anthropological epistemic shifts: subverting pernicious stereotypes, opening up horizons of possibility, and rendering the familiar strange. I demonstrate this with reference to World Hypnosis Convention , a collage of AI images that I developed for a public exhibition following long‐term fieldwork on the social imagination of hypnosis. While English‐language prompts generated highly standardized portraits of male stage performers, other languages elicited vivid, unexpected portraits that challenged rigid definitions of “hypnosis,” drew attention to the constitutive role of suggestion in social life, and invited critical perspectives on social institutions. World Hypnosis Convention thus demonstrates how AI images can support practices of anthropological exhibiting, while illuminating several limitations of AI image generation itself. In particular, it highlights the linguistic inequalities with which AI users can be faced: non‐English speakers may struggle to achieve the precision they may desire, whereas English speakers can miss out on lateral perspectives. Both issues warrant greater attention in critical anthropologies of AI and in future AI design.
