items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Spinal Diagnostics: Advances, Challenges and Future Directions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Journal of Orthopaedic Science and Research
items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in spinal diagnostics, particularly through machine learning and deep learning applied to medical imaging and clinical data. These technologies may improve the detection and classification of spinal disorders, automate image interpretation and support clinical decision-making. This narrative review summarizes current applications of AI in spinal diagnostics, focusing on methods for detecting spinal cord injuries, spinal tumors, degenerative spine diseases and vertebral fractures, as well as predicting treatment outcomes and postoperative complications. It also examines convolutional and recurrent neural networks, automated image segmentation and other machine learning approaches for analyzing spinal images and clinical information. Available evidence suggests that AI models can perform comparably to conventional methods and expert assessments and may exceed them in some settings. However, implementation remains limited by challenges related to dataset quality and diversity, model generalizability and interpretability, data privacy and regulatory and ethical considerations. This review highlights both the clinical potential of AI and the major barriers to its integration into routine spinal diagnostic practice. Further prospective validation, external testing across diverse patient populations and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to establish the clinical utility and ensure the safe implementation of AI-based spinal diagnostic tools.

items.title: Cognitive Predictors of AI-Related Textual Change in Upper-Intermediate L2 Russian Writing: Working Memory, Attention Control, and Critical Thinking

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can alter final second-language (L2) texts, yet cognitive differences may shape which changes emerge. This exploratory study examined 38 upper-intermediate learners of Russian who each produced one composition with AI assistance and one without it. Working memory, attention control, and critical thinking were measured continuously, and 11 textual outcomes were calculated from paired compositions. AI-assisted texts showed higher lemma-based lexical-diversity values, longer words, more connectives per 100 words, and substantially fewer first-person markers, while total word count, sentence measures, and formulaic-expression rate did not differ in the full sample. The higher POS-based content-word density was attenuated after first-person forms were excluded, suggesting a contribution from the change in person marking. Exploratory models suggested negative working-memory associations with lexical-diversity and connective-rate change, and negative attention-control associations with lexical-diversity change. The positive working-memory coefficient for word-count change was sensitive to HC3 estimation and leave-one-out refitting. Critical thinking showed no clear independent association in the primary change-score models, while positive coefficients for MATTR and HD-D appeared in the outcome-conditioned models. Under this supervised, student-mediated procedure, AI assistance was associated with lexical, discourse-marking, and stance differences in completed L2 texts.

items.abstract_text: Background Regulatory entry and public experience describe different aspects of artificial intelligence-enabled healthcare access. Methods This health policy study compares institutional arrangements in China, the United States, and the European Union, examines the coverage of equity-related evidence, and analyses an online Chinese survey. Of 480 submissions, 430 passed an attention check, including 32 respondents without reported functional contact and 398 entering the experience models. Results The institutional comparison identifies differences in regulatory objects, information recipients, and responsibility allocation. The coverage analysis distinguishes institutional information and hospital governance from measured portal use and service experience. In the survey, lower-capability respondents reported greater entry and operational barriers; 79 of 159 reported reducing or abandoning use because of barriers. Among contacted respondents, functional contact intensity was positively associated with perceived process ease (standardized β = 0.496), which was associated with perceived health-service responsiveness (standardized β = 0.381). The contact-by-capability interaction was negative (B = −0.254), contrary to the hypothesized direction. Conclusion The findings highlight entry and operational barriers alongside differences in experience among existing users, supporting evaluation of both access conditions and service encounters.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and the erosion of professional autonomy in clinical practice – a review and analysis

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Professional autonomy is a foundational ethical principle in healthcare, underpinning healthcare professionals’ capacity to exercise independent clinical judgement in light of a patient's particular circumstances, preferences and needs. While ethical debate surrounding medical AI has focused extensively on safety, accuracy and bias, its implications for professional autonomy have received comparatively less attention, a notable omission given AI's growing role in shaping clinical decision-making. This article identifies three salient mechanisms through which AI integration may constrain professional autonomy: (1) algorithmic opacity and explainability, (2) automation bias and de-skilling and (3) institutional pressures. Whilst proposed safeguards such as explainable AI, professional training, system design and institutional governance represent important directions, they do not yet adequately protect professional autonomy. This article therefore calls for closer scrutiny of current approaches to AI integration and for governance frameworks that attend not only to the technical properties of AI systems, but to the organisational and institutional conditions in which they are deployed.

items.title: CHATGPT USE AND PERCEIVED IMPROVEMENT IN ENGLISH SPEAKING: EVIDENCE FROM ENGLISH-MAJOR STUDENTS  AT A VIETNAMESE UNIVERSITY

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.venue: Tạp chí Nghiên cứu Chính sách và Phát triển
items.abstract_text: This study examined the relationship between ChatGPT use and English-major students’ perceived improvement in English speaking. It focused on three aspects of ChatGPT use: frequency of use, speaking purposes, and interaction level. Data were collected from 238 English-major students at the Academy of Policy and Development in Vietnam using a 5-point Likert-scale questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, exploratory factor analysis, Pearson correlation, and multiple regression were used for data analysis. The results showed positive associations between all three aspects of ChatGPT use and perceived improvement. Speaking purposes had the strongest association (r = .709), followed by interaction level (r = .699) and frequency of use (r = .614), with all p < .001. The multiple regression model was statistically significant, F(3, 234) = 239.977, p < .001, with the three predictors accounting for 75.5% of the variance in perceived improvement. Speaking purposes (β = .397), interaction level (β = .382), and frequency of use (β = .336) were significant predictors of perceived improvement. Students also reported relatively high perceived improvement across the five speaking dimensions, with fluency receiving the highest mean score (M = 4.01). Given the cross-sectional and self-reported nature of the data, the findings indicate statistical associations rather than causal effects.

items.abstract_text: Sentiment analysis has become a fundamental task in natural language processing to extract public opinions from social media and online review platforms at a large scale. Recent machine learning, deep learning and transformer-based approaches have been significantly improved for sentiment classification. However, these models are still suffering from high-dimensional feature representations, redundant contextual information and unstable feature learning, which limit the classification accuracy and model generalization. To solve these problems, this paper proposes an Optimization-Guided Feature Refinement and Adaptive Attention RoBERTa (OGFAA-RoBERTa). OGFAA-RoBERTa reduced the feature dimensionality by an optimization-based feature selection technique and improved the model stability by a deep contextual feature extraction strategy. The OGFAA-RoBERTa incorporates preprocessing of data, optimization-guided feature refinement, adaptive attention learning and enhanced RoBERTa classifier to learn highly discriminative semantic representation while suppressing redundant contextual features. Experimental evaluation was performed on Sentiment140 and SemEval-2014 datasets. The OGFAA-RoBERTa achieves 92.34% accuracy on Sentiment140 and 88.76%, 92.43% and 85.74% on the Laptop14, Restaurant14 and Twitter subsets of SemEval-2014, respectively. The results show that the optimization-guided feature refinement and the adaptive attention can significantly improve the performance of sentiment classification, model stability and cross-domain generalization over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

items.abstract_text: Against digital education background, generative AI has become common writing assistance for undergraduates. Existing studies mainly focus on second-language writing and ignore stratified comparisons across learners, while the dual effects of AI on academic writing self-efficacy remain understudied. Based on self-efficacy theory, this paper distributes questionnaires and divides respondents into three proficiency groups by CET-4 scores. Descriptive statistics, group difference tests and correlation analysis are adopted for empirical analysis. The results reveal prevalent AI over-dependence despite its polishing functions. Participants’ writing self-efficacy stays at medium-upper level yet hampered by writing anxiety. AI delivers short-term confidence promotion but impairs independent writing competence in the long run, with stronger influences on low-proficiency students. This stratified dual-path framework offers empirical references for standardized AI application in university writing teaching.

items.abstract_text: AI's most important wellbeing dividend may not come from producing more output, but from changing the composition of economic life. By reducing the administrative, cognitive, financial, and procedural burdens that absorb human capacity without building capability, AI can dissolve forms of extractive friction. But unless the resulting gains are protected from rent migration and redirected into formative infrastructure, extraction will not disappear; it will reappear in AI-native form. This paper develops a compositional theory of AI and wellbeing, distinguishing the philosophical hinge between extractive friction (burdens that drain capacity without building it) and formative friction (difficulty that develops judgment, skill, relationship, and responsibility). The wellbeing dividend is mapped across four BANI channels, with Brittleness treated explicitly as a hypothesis-generating channel rather than an established mechanism. The paper distinguishes theory from prescription. The prescription is a triadic policy mechanism: dissolution compresses extractive friction; anti-recapture prevents migrated rents from forming a new layer of extraction (taxation is its principal fiscal instance, alongside interoperability mandates, fiduciary duties, antitrust scrutiny, and public AI provision); and formation funding directs released capacity into relational and developmental infrastructure. The triad is operationalised through a five-test evaluative toolkit (Capability, Proportionality, Distribution, Migration, Formation) designed to assess whether any AI deployment or proposed policy actually advances compositional change rather than merely automating the existing equilibrium.

items.abstract_text: AI-mediated teaching requires teachers to evaluate uncertain information, respond to changing conditions, and integrate AI with pedagogical judgment. This study examined four cognitive-professional resource domains relevant to intelligent professional action: digital literacy, digital resilience, AI-mediated epistemic agency (AMEA), and AI-TPACK. Variable-centered and person-centered analyses drew on a cross-sectional survey of 942 YouShi Plan preservice teachers at one Chinese university. Perceived structured teacher-education support was positively associated with all four resources. Self-reported teaching innovation competence was positively associated with jointly higher digital literacy and digital resilience, with the response surface primarily reflecting their combined level. Four resource profiles mainly differed in overall level and showed graded differences in perceived teaching innovation competence. Higher perceived support was also associated with membership in higher-resource profiles. Together, these findings connect perceived teacher-education support, cognitive-professional resource configurations, and self-reported teaching innovation competence, positioning the latter as a domain-specific perceived capability relevant to intelligent professional action in AI-mediated teaching.

items.title: Evaluating the AI-predictive potential of the PIC database for pediatric ICU mortality

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background Reliable Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in healthcare depend on both data quality and model design. However, the predictive integrity of datasets is rarely assessed. Publicly available resources for critically ill children remain scarce. The Pediatric Intensive Care (PIC) database remains, to the best of current knowledge, the only open-access resource focused on pediatric critical care research. Methods This study evaluates the predictive potential of the PIC database. After applying strict cohort selection and data preprocessing, mortality risk was analyzed using statistical analysis through univariate Odds Ratio (OR) to measure associations, and machine learning (ML) models interpreted through SHAP values to assess feature importance and model behavior. Results ML experiments showed moderate but limited predictive performance for mortality. CatBoost performed best, with an AUC of 0.8521 (0.8414–0.8627) on the hold-out test set, but low sensitivity (42%) limited its ability to identify non-survivors. These findings suggest dataset-related constraints that reduce clinical reliability. Most relevant variables were minimum lactate, maximum lactate, mean respiratory rate, maximum hematocrit, and minimum urea. Conclusion Analysis showed that PIC lacks essential physiological data, highlighting the limits of current pediatric databases and the need for richer multicenter datasets to enable more robust, clinically applicable AI models. Impact Provides the first comprehensive evaluation of the PIC database, assessing its suitability for machine learning-based predictive modeling. Identifies key clinical variables and data gaps that influence the reliability of AI–based mortality prediction and model performance. Underscores the need for richer, multicenter pediatric ICU databases for research that incorporate essential physiological and neurological indicators. Demonstrates the value of combining statistical association and AI interpretability methods to assess the predictive integrity of clinical datasets.

reading.methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study using the PIC database. 13 PIC comprises 13,499 hospital admissions from 12,881 unique pediatric patients (aged 0-18 years) admitted to Children's Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine between 2010 and 2018. It contains more than 1,298 variables derived from deidentified patient records, including vital signs, laboratory tests, medications, fluid balance, diagnostic codes, and other bedside clinical data. All patient identifiers were removed in compliance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), and access to the database is restricted to users who complete human-subjects research training and sign a data use agreement, thereby ensuring ethical and responsible data use. The PIC database is organized into 16 interlinked tables. For the present study, "PATIENTS", "ADMISSIONS", and "ICUSTAYS" tables were used to obtain and integrate key demographic, admission, and ICU-stay information. All files are provided in comma-separated value (CSV) format, which facilitates their use in relational database systems.

This predominance should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence that laboratory measurements are intrinsically more clinically relevant than physiological variables. It may also reflect the availability, completeness, and representation of different variable types within the PIC database. The ML results further support this interpretation. items.abstract_text: ABSTRACT Preparing preservice teachers for AI‐enabled teaching requires understanding anxiety alongside perceived capability and self‐regulated learning (SRL). Drawing on data from 12,147 third‐year preservice teachers across 17 Chinese institutions, this study combined structural equation modelling, observed‐score moderation, and latent profile analysis. Four profiles emerged: the Moderate Profile, the Lower‐Efficacy, Lower‐SRL Profile, the Low‐Anxiety, Higher‐SRL Profile, and the High‐Anxiety, Higher‐SRL Profile. The two higher‐SRL profiles shared high ICT self‐efficacy despite contrasting anxiety levels. AI anxiety was positively associated with ICT self‐efficacy, which was strongly associated with SRL. items.title: THE AI LEARNING PARADOX: REVEALING HOW UNIVERSITY STUDENTS NAVIGATE LEARNING CONVENIENCE, COGNITIVE EFFORT, DIGITAL CONTENT INFLUENCE, ACADEMIC CONFIDENCE, AND EDUCATIONAL ENGAGEMENT

items.abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has introduced a significant paradox in higher education by simultaneously enhancing learning accessibility, personalization, and academic confidence while creating concerns regarding reduced cognitive effort and technological dependency. This study explores how university students navigate AI-supported learning experiences by examining five key dimensions: learning convenience, cognitive effort, digital content influence, academic confidence, and educational engagement. Adopting a qualitative research design, the study investigates the lived experiences of 18 Pakistani university students through semi-structured interviews. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis to identify patterns within students’ perceptions and practices of AI use. The findings reveal six major themes: AI as an educational accelerator, convenience versus intellectual struggle, confidence versus competence, transformation of digital learning consumption, risks of AI dependency, and purposeful AI-supported learning. The study demonstrates that AI can enhance educational engagement when used as a cognitive partner but may weaken independent learning when relied upon excessively. The findings highlight the importance of AI literacy, responsible technology integration, and pedagogical strategies that preserve students’ cognitive autonomy while maximizing the benefits of AI in higher education.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background and aims With the rapid development of conversational artificial intelligence (CAI), problematic use of conversational AI (PUCAI) among adolescents has attracted increasing attention. However, the underlying psychological factors associated with PUCAI remain unclear. Guided by the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, this study explored the associations between interpersonal alienation, perceived anthropomorphism, AI attachment, and PUCAI. Methods Data were collected from 1,124 Chinese high school students (516 males, 608 females; M age = 16.59). Serial mediation analysis and network analysis were conducted. Results Interpersonal alienation was positively associated with PUCAI. It also had indirect associations through both parallel and serial mediation involving perceived anthropomorphism and AI attachment. Network analysis further revealed that perceived anthropomorphism exhibited the highest bridge expected influence, and emotional trust showed the highest centrality. Conclusion These findings suggest that adolescent PUCAI is associated not only with general psychological risk factors but also with social-cognitive perceptions and emotional bonding experiences during human–AI interactions. This study provides a novel perspective for understanding problematic use behaviors in emerging human–AI interaction contexts and offers implications for future risk assessment and research on healthy AI use.

items.abstract_text: Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into university learning, raising questions about dependency-oriented reliance and self-regulation. Drawing on a self-regulated learning perspective, this study examined associations among GenAI dependency, effort regulation, and multidimensional perceived learning outcomes, including the statistical indirect association involving effort regulation. Methods Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 982 students at three higher education institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling were conducted, with indirect associations tested using 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for GenAI use frequency. Results The measurement model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.043, SRMR = 0.041). GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = −0.087) and was negatively associated with effort regulation ( β = −0.257). Effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.497). The residual direct association was nonsignificant ( β = 0.041), whereas the indirect association was negative and significant ( β = −0.128). After adjustment for GenAI use frequency, the indirect association remained significant, but the small total association was no longer significant. Conclusion The findings highlight effort regulation as a relevant learner-controlled process in the association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. They also distinguish dependency-oriented reliance from frequency of GenAI use. The cross-sectional design and potential classroom clustering warrant cautious interpretation.

analysis.discussion: The present study examined the associations among generative AI dependency, effort regulation, and perceived learning outcomes among university students. GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes and was negatively associated with effort regulation, whereas effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes. The overall negative association included a statistically significant negative indirect component involving effort regulation, while the residual direct association was small, positive in sign, and not statistically significant. The primary latent-variable model indicated a small negative total association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. Although this association was statistically significant under the assumption of independent observations, its magnitude was limited ( β = −0.087), and the upper bound of its confidence interval was close to zero. The result therefore suggests only a modest relationship at the individual level and should not be interpreted as evidence of a substantial educational disadvantage associated with GenAI dependency. Moreover, because potential clustering within instructional classes was not accounted for, the precision of the estimated association may have been overstated. After effort regulation was included in the structural model, the residual direct association was not statistically significant. This pattern should not be interpreted as demonstrating that effort regulation fully explains the overall association or that the observed indirect association represents a causal mechanism. Previous research has associated GenAI dependency with procrastination, cognitive failures, poorer task performance, and weaker critical thinking ( Goh et al., 2025 ), while greater AI dependence has also been associated with lower critical thinking among university students ( Tian and Zhang, 2025 ). AI over-reliance has likewise been linked to less favorable learning performance ( Gao et al., 2026 ). However, these outcomes are not equivalent to perceived learning. The present study assessed students’ perceived cognitive, behavioral, and affective learning gains rather than objectively demonstrated achievement. Because perceived learning and independently assessed performance may diverge ( Deslauriers et al., 2019 ), the findings cannot establish whether GenAI dependency is similarly associated with objective learning outcomes. The present data cannot fully disentangle these subjective and objective dimensions, and the nonsignificant residual direct association should not be interpreted as evidence that GenAI dependency is educationally inconsequential. GenAI dependency was negatively associated with effort regulation, consistent with emerging evidence connecting AI dependency with self-regulatory functioning. items.abstract_text: AI has permeated all facets of life, society and economy. This article purports to evaluate the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the Indian Healthcare landscape with particular reference to geriatric healthcare. The paper focuses on the silver divide and the scope it offers for health care providers who can leverage a growing elderly care segment. The study also presents the current AI based interventions in the health care for the aged and their alignment to the relevant sustainable development goals. The strategic opportunities offered by the silver economy, funding support from government and private players, governmental interventions and the regulatory framework along with ethical considerations are also discussed in this paper.

items.title: Investigating Patient Trust and Intention to Act in AI-Supported Clinical Decisions: Cross-Sectional Survey

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract Background In health systems, AI is increasingly being implemented as a form of clinical decision support (CDS). Research on patient perspectives, however, lags behind clinician-focused studies. Before the introduction of AI-based tools, clinicians often used and continue to use rule-based guidelines and risk calculators (RCs) to inform decision-making. Prior research has shown that RCs for CDS have mixed effects on patient adherence to treatment recommendations, whereas for AI-based tools, the effect is still not clear. Objective This study aims to assess differences in patients’ behavioral intentions, trust, and preferences for clinical recommendations provided by doctors alone, doctors supported by RCs, and doctors supported by AI-based risk predictions. We also evaluate how sociodemographic characteristics affect these perceptions. Methods We surveyed 1185 US-based adults. Participants rated their likelihood of taking recommended clinical actions (behavioral intentions) across 6 clinical scenarios, where they were randomized to a different recommendation source (doctor, doctor + RC, and doctor + AI). Participants also rated their trust in the recommendation, indicated their preferred source for recommendations, and provided qualitative feedback. Results Behavioral intentions differed by recommendation source such that the doctor + RC condition had greater odds of behavioral intention than the doctor + AI condition. Behavioral intentions were also affected by the clinical condition. Participants had greater odds of trusting doctors alone over doctor + RC, and both doctors alone and doctor + RC had greater trust than doctor + AI. However, a plurality of participants ultimately preferred a doctor using an RC for making recommendations. Several sociodemographic differences were detected, namely, participants with higher subjective numeracy and literacy had higher odds of taking clinical action and higher trust across decision-support sources. We detected qualitative themes in the following categories: decision quality and reliability; trust and perceptions; patient-centeredness and autonomy; fairness, transparency, and ethics. Across categories, participants reported skepticism toward all decision sources and potential misunderstanding of AI’s ability to personalize risk predictions. Some participants also stated that they had no additional concerns or were uncertain regarding their feelings. Conclusions These findings reveal novel, nuanced patient preferences shaped by task and context, offering guidance for aligning AI-supported care with patient values. Patients were not aligned on the recommendation source across intentions, trust, and preferences. Taken together, our results indicate that patients prefer doctors working with easy-to-understand, explainable support but are still learning to trust these tools. Our findings also highlight the continued importance of the clinical context and its interaction with computer-assisted decision support. Future work should evaluate how we can transparently convey to patients the use of AI in clinical decision-making, embedded within the given clinical context. This may present an opportunity to bolster, rather than erode, patient trust.

analysis.methods: We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of US-based adults between June 17, 2024, and July 26, 2024. We recruited participants via Qualtrics’ survey sampling service, which drew respondents to the closed survey from an opt-in online panel. Eligibility criteria included being at least 18 years of age, being able to read English, and providing informed consent within the Qualtrics platform before beginning the survey. No personal information that would allow identification of participants was collected during the survey. To support comparisons across sociodemographic groups, we used quota sampling balanced on sex, education (with vs without a bachelor’s degree or higher), and generation (Baby Boomer, Generation X [Gen X], Millennial, and Generation Z [Gen Z]). We also targeted approximately half of the sample to identify as members of racial or ethnic minority groups. Participants were given monetary compensation for participating in the survey. The Columbia University Institutional Review Board approved this study (IRB review number: AAAU3382). The design and results of the survey are reported in accordance with the CHERRIES (Checklist for Reporting Results of Internet E-Surveys) guidelines ( Checklist 1 ) [ 29 ]. We developed survey items with input from experts in human factors, anthropology, human-centered AI, AI development, nursing, primary care, and survey design. Our team iteratively drafted and refined the items through multiple rounds of pilot testing with both experts and laypersons to assess comprehensibility and face validity. Excluding unavoidable technical terms (eg, “artificial intelligence” and clinical vocabulary), we targeted an eighth-grade reading level. The full survey battery of questions used during data collection is provided in Multimedia Appendix 1 . The results of the generative AI questions that appear in the survey are not included in this paper. After confirming age eligibility and obtaining consent, demographic questions were used to determine whether respondents met current quota needs. Those proceeding to the survey received definitions of “risk calculators” and “artificial intelligence,” and confirmed their understanding. Definitions stated: Risk calculators allow doctors, nurses, and patients to enter information about a patient (such as, age, gender, smoking status) and calculate a number that shows a patient’s risk, for example, of having a stroke (see picture below). These tools can easily explain how they get to the risk prediction because they use simple math . Artificial intelligence (AI) or “AI,” refers to computer programs that can learn to make decisions or predictions like humans using large amounts of data. AI, for example, may take large amounts of data from patients they know did and did not have a stroke in their lifetime. The AI learns patterns from this data and predicts who is at high risk of stroke in the future. AI is different from a risk calculator in that it cannot always explain the rules it used to make a prediction . Participants were asked about their behavioral intentions, trust, and preferences regarding medical decisions made by (1) a doctor alone, (2) a doctor supported by an RC, and (3) a doctor supported by AI. Each participant viewed six clinical scenarios (lung cancer, sepsis, depression, colon cancer, respiratory syncytial virus [RSV] vaccination, and heart failure). Participants were randomly assigned to 1 of 6 blocks, which included each decision source in 2 of the 6 scenarios and each clinical condition once, with no decision source repeated immediately on consecutive scenarios. The order of clinical conditions and decision sources was partially balanced to mitigate ordering effects. This process is illustrated in Textbox 1 . Each scenario included a brief description of the condition (adapted from MedlinePlus patient education materials) [ 30 ], followed by items assessing intended behavior and trust in the recommendation ( Table 1 ). After completing all scenarios, participants indicated their preferred CDS approach (doctor alone, doctor + RC, or doctor + AI) for each condition. Participants were then invited to provide qualitative feedback about their concerns regarding each decision-support approach. Before completing the survey, participants answered additional demographic measures on subjective numeracy (3-item Subjective Numeracy Scale) [ 31 ], health literacy (3-item Brief Health Literacy Screen) [ 32 ], perceived financial stability, comfort with the use of technology, and perceived discrimination in medical settings (7-item Discrimination in Medical Settings scale) [ 33 ]. We powered the study to detect differences in behavioral intentions across the 3 CDS conditions (doctor alone, doctor + RC, doctor + AI). Based on prior AI-related acceptability studies, we considered a 15% absolute difference (approximately a medium effect size; odds ratio [OR] 1.94) to be practically significant ( α =.05; β =.80). Using these parameters in R (version 4.5.0; R Foundation for Statistical Computing), we estimated a minimum of 256 participants per decision-support group (n=768). We set 768 as the minimum target and allowed additional enrollment to facilitate subgroup analyses. Our analyses focused on racial groups constituting 5% of the total sample, rounded to the nearest percentage point. analysis.discussion: Our study provides evidence regarding patient perspectives on realistic, yet hypothetical, implementations of AI-informed CDS. Prior work has not examined, within a single comparative study, patients’ reactions to common sources of CDS: a clinician working alone; a clinician using rule-based tools or guidelines (eg, RCs); and a clinician receiving AI support. A 2021 study found that patient participants were more likely to follow recommendations from a doctor alone or a doctor using AI than from an AI system making decisions independently, though this has been one of the few studies to quantitatively compare these decision-support options [ 21 ]. In our study, decision source perspectives for behavioral intentions, trust, and preference did not align. Participants reported being likely to take a clinical action (behavioral intention) more often in the doctor + risk score scenarios than in the doctor + AI scenarios. However, participants expressed the greatest trust in doctor-alone scenarios, followed by doctor + RC, and were least trusting of doctor + AI. Yet, similar to behavioral intentions, participants preferred the doctor + RC–informed decisions. This divergence between intentions, trust, and preferences may suggest that patients may want clinicians to leverage external, evidence-based tools that can synthesize complex information, yet they remain cautious about tools explicitly labeled as “AI,” although this hypothesis requires further investigation. We found some consistent and some divergent patterns across behavioral intentions and trust related to the impact of the clinical condition; participants had lower behavioral intentions and trust in the depression (psychiatry referral) and heart failure (go home instead of being admitted) scenarios compared to the sepsis reference scenario. On the other hand, participants had lower behavioral intentions but higher trust for the colon cancer scenarios compared to sepsis. It is important to note that the sepsis scenario involved a proxy decision for a loved one. While it may be challenging to derive conclusive insights on AI use in specific clinical scenarios, our findings do underscore the continued importance of the clinical context and recommended action. We found differences in both behavioral intentions and trust in certain sociodemographic groups; however, since these analyses were conducted across decision support conditions, they provide more insight into clinical decision-making in general, rather than computer-supported clinical decision-making. Findings reflect what may be anticipated based on prior work related to trust in medical care [ 38 , 39 ]. For example, those who reported experiencing greater discrimination in medical settings also reported lower trust in decision-making regardless of decision support condition. Higher self-rated health literacy and numeracy were also associated with greater trust and behavioral intentions. Future studies may benefit from exploring a single clinical scenario and assessing the interaction between different decision support conditions and sociodemographic characteristics to better understand how participant characteristics may impact perspectives on computer-supported decision support. Qualitative responses echoed prior literature on reliability, trust, personalization, and bias [ 40 ], while adding a side-by-side critique of both computer-supported and human decision-making. Comments revealed interest in transparency in both humans (doctors being influenced by pharmaceutical or other financial incentives) and AI (lack of explanation of results). Participants described doubts and perceived deficiencies for each decision source, reinforcing the idea that all approaches have trade-offs and appropriate use cases. Qualitative findings revealed a potential misconception that AI cannot personalize care. In fact, predictive models can incorporate large volumes of patient-specific data and dynamically adjust variable weights, but this capability is not intuitive to patients. While a substantial share of participants reported no additional concerns (40.4% for clinicians, 42.5% for RCs, and 31.1% for AI), a smaller subset expressed genuine uncertainty of opinion (1.8%, 4.0%, and 3.7%, respectively). This latter group, combined with the potential misconception around AI’s personalization capabilities described above, suggests that gaps in understanding of how AI tools work persist for at least a portion of patients, even as most did not report active concerns. Our findings offer future avenues of investigation for implementing AI in clinically realistic ways. While AI-related safety concerns must be continuously monitored and mitigated, AI can deliver benefits in predictive performance and clinical efficiency. To preserve trust, these benefits should be communicated to patients clearly and transparently. Qualitative findings highlight the potential value of simplified, inclusive, and digestible general patient-facing education about AI. Many participants wanted to learn how AI works and how it supports their health. Comments about a lack of personalization suggest gaps in understanding AI’s capabilities and limits. Videos and tutorials that explain basic AI concepts may be an engaging starting point; they can be adapted to health care with a strong emphasis on safety and appropriate use. Although the AI decision source did not change participants’ stated likelihood of following recommended clinical actions, we observed lower trust in clinicians supported by AI for predictive tasks and stronger preferences for rule-based “risk calculators” with easily explainable outputs. Given ethical obligations and legal initiatives [ 6 , 7 ], it is important to disclose when AI supports treatment recommendations. To avoid eroding trust, disclosures should provide context-specific information about the tools used. This can include information such as how and when the AI adds value beyond human judgment, performance on representative populations, data provenance and uncertainty, and assurances that clinicians remain in control. In alignment with prior work, information should make system capabilities and limitations visible and support efficient correction and oversight [ 41 ]. These and previous results suggest that information should also be tailored to the clinical condition, as people value actionable, question-driven transparency over generic disclosures [ 42 ]. Implementation may benefit from reusable design patterns and templates that can be customized to the site and clinical context. Providing Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources–based components and detailed implementation guides may support scalability across settings. Participants appeared more receptive to terms like “risk calculator” than “AI.” They also valued explainability, underscoring the importance of patient-facing explanations (eg, salient features or illustrative examples). Our study was also conducted only with adults in the United States. We were also unable to account for previous experiences with particular clinical conditions, which may have influenced the trust and behavioral intentions of individual respondents. Moreover, as the scenarios involved hypothetical medical decisions rather than actual care decisions, the participants’ responses could differ when compared with a real-world setting. Future work should assess similar research questions in other settings and may also benefit from understanding how patients’ lived experiences concretely affect their perspectives. We also did not formally test for order or carryover effects across the six scenarios; while our design prevented consecutive repetition of the same recommendation source, future work could examine whether scenario position influenced responses.

items.abstract_text: While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies such as conversational chatbots and speech recognition systems are increasingly adopted in language education, existing research focuses predominantly on isolated tools rather than integrated instructional models. This study proposes and evaluates a Human–AI Collaborative Blended Learning Framework for the development of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) speaking skills. Using a two-phase research design, the study first synthesizes contemporary literature to establish a 7-layer conceptual framework that connects stakeholder participation, learner profiling, a Human–AI collaboration engine, blended activities, adaptive speaking services, teacher facilitation, and continuous learning analytics. Second, the framework was evaluated through an expert validation survey involving 52 specialists in language education, applied linguistics, and educational technology (40.4% PhDs, 57.7% Master’s). Quantitative findings revealed strong endorsement for actionable teacher support dashboards (80.8% agreement), visual pronunciation feedback (78.8%), and private AI speaking practice for anxiety reduction (75.0%; M = 2.98/4.00). However, experts expressed reservations regarding automated prompts for language elaboration (53.8% agreement), fixed 14-meeting schedules (57.7%), and automated grading weights (57.7%). Qualitative analysis highlighted that acceptance remains conditional upon accent fairness, data privacy, and active teacher oversight. Implications: Theoretically, the study advances AI-assisted language learning by establishing a human-centered collaborative model that prioritizes teacher-AI shared regulation over technological substitution. Pedagogically and practically, the findings imply that institutions and EdTech developers should deploy AI primarily for scalable, low-stakes rehearsal and actionable lesson planning, while preserving teacher authority over social communication, pragmatic competence, and high-stakes assessment.

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being integrated into educational practices, transforming how students access information, develop ideas, and carry out cognitive tasks. While GenAI offers opportunities to foster critical thinking and creativity, its use raises concerns regarding "cognitive offloading"—the delegation of reasoning processes that are fundamental to learning. This study presents a review based on 108 documents from Scopus and Web of Science, which allowed for an examination of the relationships between GenAI, critical thinking, creativity, and cognitive offloading, as well as their pedagogical and institutional implications. The evidence analyzed suggests that GenAI can improve immediate task performance, facilitate idea generation, and support content development. However, these benefits do not necessarily translate into autonomous learning or greater creative originality. Outcomes appear to depend on students' prior knowledge, their AI literacy, task design, metacognitive regulation, and the nature and timing of pedagogical support. Based on this review, an AI-Mediated Cognitive Infrastructure Framework (AMCIF) is proposed, which links GenAI usage patterns with cognitive processes, educational practices, and institutional conditions. This framework distinguishes between forms of assistance that promote cognitive engagement and those that might replace the mental activity necessary for learning, emphasizing the essential role of instructor mediation, source verification, reflective practices, and process-oriented assessment. The AMCIF provides a conceptual foundation for analyzing how to integrate GenAI into educational settings while preserving critical judgment, creativity, and the capacity for independent reasoning. The proposed relationships require rigorous empirical validation.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative AI (GenAI) has rapidly moved from novelty to ubiquity, reshaping how doctoral students approach learning, research, and career preparation. Yet while universities and the public often frame debates around undergraduate use, comparatively little attention has been given to PhD students despite their dual role as learners and future scholars. In this paper, we reflect on our experiences as PhD students using GenAI across coursework, qualifying exams, thesis research, teaching, and the job market. Drawing on these experiences, we highlight both the opportunities GenAI provides—for efficiency, conceptual clarity, and skill development—and the ethical challenges it raises, including concerns about academic integrity, cognitive outsourcing, disclosure, and employability beyond academia. Our reflections emphasize that GenAI use is not uniform: it varies with disciplinary context, institutional policies, and students’ levels of development. We argue that GenAI is no longer peripheral to doctoral education but central to its practice, and the challenge ahead is how it can be integrated responsibly to support learning, uphold integrity, and prepare graduates for an evolving academic and professional landscape.

items.title: Enhancing Students' Critical Evaluation of AI Versus Human-Generated Literature Reviews: Deliberative Pedagogy

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Background: AI misuse in literature reviews has emerged as an issue for educators. The goal of this teaching innovation was to foster learners' critical thinking about AI use in literature reviews. Method: A four-step deliberative pedagogical process was applied: (a) announcing literature review battles between AI and humans, (b) presenting review results generated by both sides, (c) using a poll to ask learners to choose their preferred review results for policy decision-making, and (d) debriefing on the speed and accuracy of both reviews. Results: Sixty-one learners responded to the poll: 51% ( n = 31) chose human-generated reviews, 36% ( n = 22) chose AI-generated reviews, while 13% ( n = 8) expressed their surprise at AI's performance. Debriefing showed that AI spent only 0.5 hours completing the review, but with low search accuracy, whereas humans achieved high accuracy but took more than 6 months. Conclusion: Deliberative pedagogy encourages learners to recalibrate their AI knowledge and reconsider the importance of human decision-making in literature reviews.

items.title: Human-Led AI-In-The-Loop Drift Forecasting for Faster Marine Casualty Response

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Summary When a vessel loses propulsion it becomes a drift-dominated casualty, and the response team must begin preparing decisions on towage, refuge, authority notification and specialist salvage engagement before the casualty picture is complete. The information available in the first hour rarely supports the decisions that must be made in the first hour. This paper presents a human-led, staged workflow for early-stage drift assessment and argues that loss-of-propulsion drift should be treated as a defined scenario in the marine operational risk register rather than as an improvised emergency calculation. The workflow makes two contributions: a Stage 0 pre-casualty readiness concept, in which methodology, data sources and escalation logic are prepared in advance; and a staged live process that converts fragmentary, uneven-confidence information into an indicative drift sector and bounded speed band, and connects that picture to response decisions through a decision margin that compares the earliest credible hazard-arrival time with the required response lead time. Drift is estimated by a transparent three-component velocity decomposition with explicit low, base and high scenarios; automatic identification system (AIS) data are used to refine and sense-check the estimate, and artificial intelligence (AI) serves as an organising and consistency-checking layer while technical interpretation and operational authority remain with qualified people. The approach is demonstrated on an anonymised disabled tanker in the northern Arabian Sea, assessed in fallback mode without a pre-prepared Stage 0 readiness file. The initial assessment indicated a drift sector of approximately 119–122°T and a speed band of approximately 0.8–2.0 kn; subsequent AIS movement remained within the broad assessed sector and towards the upper end of the speed band, while exposing the information gaps that pre-casualty readiness is intended to reduce. The case is a single real-condition demonstration, not a statistical validation of the method.

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Abstract The objective of this work is to demonstrate the successful deployment of a secure, AI-driven closed-loop automation system for LNG plant pre-cooldown. The scope encompasses the transition from a data-driven advisory model to a fully autonomous system that executes real-time valve adjustments. It focuses on achieving critical outcomes in enabling autonomous, real-time adjustments through AI-driven recommendations, minimizing startup duration variability, maximizing additional production hours and reducing greenhouse gas emissions through optimized thermodynamic control. The methodology utilized twenty-five years of historical startup data, which was cleaned and profiled to train supervised machine learning models that predict Main Cryogenic Heat Exchanger (MCHE) temperature profiles and valve responses. These predictive models were integrated with an advanced optimization layer to define precise control sequences that satisfy safe operating envelopes. A cyber-resilient IT-OT architecture was engineered, employing network segmentation and protocol gateways to bridge the plant network and the AI engine securely. The process followed a phased validation: initial deployment as a "live advisory" to calibrate model accuracy, followed by the activation of a closed-loop controller that executes autonomous valve adjustments with human-in-the-loop safeguards. The system was successfully deployed across eight LNG train startups at Malaysia LNG plant. Quantitative results confirm a 16% average reduction in pre-cooldown duration compared to the live-advisory baseline. This acceleration directly translates into increased production availability and the reduction of operators' workloads, which allows operators to focus on strategic overview and process safety —enhancing both safety and efficiency. Observations revealed that the closed-loop implementation successfully standardized the pre-cooldown sequence across all eight production runs, delivering near-identical, optimized cooling trajectories. Critically, the tighter control of the Main Cryogenic Heat Exchanger (MCHE) cooling curve led to a 22% reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by minimizing flaring events during the transition to stable operations. The study concludes that autonomous closed-loop systems are superior in achieving repeatable, high-efficiency startups. Furthermore, the integration of a secure IT-OT framework addresses the industry's primary barrier to AI adoption: cybersecurity in critical infrastructure. This paper provides a documented case study of an AI system moving beyond "recommendations" into "autonomous execution" in a critical energy facility. It introduces a novel, hybrid methodology combining Supervised Machine Learning with prescriptive optimization logic. This innovation highlights the transformative power of closed-loop, AI-driven automation, reinforcing the organization's leadership in operational excellence and its commitment to setting new standards for industrial processes.

The study was pilot-tested on a sample of 30 students, of whom 10 students were randomly selected from different lecture groups. With their comments and suggestions, the questionnaire was amended and subsequently used for the main data collection. The questionnaire had three sections. Part A consisted of the basic demographics: gender, age, and university level. Part B contained items measuring the UTAUT constructs of Performance Expectancy, Effort Expectancy, and Social Influence. Items measuring these constructs were adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003) and contextualized to GenAI-supported learning. The third part, Part C, contained items measuring Digital Learning Anxiety (DLA) and Behavioral Intention (BI). The DLA items were adapted from the identified literature on technology- and AI-related anxiety and contextualized to Generative AI-supported learning, while the BI items were adapted from Venkatesh et al. (2003) . All items were measured on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree). The measurement items and their corresponding sources are presented in Appendix A . Content validity was first established through expert review. The suitability of the draft instrument was assessed by three senior researchers and two lecturers in the Department of English and Linguistics. This assessment was done to check whether the items of measurement sounded ambiguous, were appropriate for the research objectives with regard to Generative AI, and whether the statements were clear to university students. From their suggestions, minor adjustments in wording were made in the items measuring Digital Learning Anxiety to make them even clearer. Following the assessment of content validity, statistical analysis through SPSS (v.23) was used to check the internal consistency of the constructs. Although Cronbach's alpha is widely reported, McDonald's Omega was adopted as the principal reliability coefficient because it provides a more robust estimate of internal consistency for latent variable models. As shown in Table 2 , the reliability analysis was conducted for the five core constructs: performance expectancy (PE), effort expectancy (EE), social influence (SI), digital learning anxiety (DLA), and behavioral intention (BI). It can be observed that all constructs demonstrated high internal consistency, with values above the commonly recommended threshold of 0.70 ( Hair et al., 2012 ). Effort Expectancy (EE) obtained the highest reliability ( ω = .969), followed by Digital Learning Anxiety ( ω = .966), Behavioral Intention ( ω = .957), and Performance Expectancy ( ω = .964). The lowest value, for Social Influence (SI), was still satisfactory at ω = .884. These results indicate satisfactory internal consistency among the items measuring the five constructs. To minimize common method bias, procedural and statistical actions were taken ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Participants were assured of their anonymity and that their answers would be treated on a confidential basis to avoid social desirability bias. In addition, the questionnaire items were separated into different sections to reduce response pattern tendencies. The single questionnaire was divided into several sections, each consisting of the corresponding items. The first unrotated factor accounted for 43.24% of the total variance. However, because Harman's single-factor test provides only a limited diagnostic of common method bias, this result was not treated as conclusive evidence that common method bias was absent ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Although procedural remedies and Harman's single-factor assessment were used to assess the possibility of common method bias, Harman's test alone cannot conclusively establish the absence of such bias. Therefore, the results should not be interpreted as demonstrating that common method bias has been completely eliminated. Exploratory Factor Analysis was conducted using the SPSS statistical package version 23. EFA was conducted to examine the underlying factor structure of the measurement items and to assess whether the observed variables loaded onto their intended latent constructs. analysis.discussion: This study examined the associations of traditional UTAUT constructs and Digital Learning Anxiety with university students’ intention to use Generative AI. The findings showed that Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy were positively associated with Behavioral Intention, whereas Digital Learning Anxiety was negatively associated with Behavioral Intention. Social Influence was not significantly associated with Behavioral Intention. These findings provide context-specific evidence that both cognitive evaluations and affective responses are relevant to understanding students’ intention to use GenAI. Among the predictors examined, Performance Expectancy had the largest positive standardized association with Behavioral Intention. This finding indicates that students primarily evaluate Generative AI based on its perceived ability to improve their academic performance. This finding is consistent with the original UTAUT model, which identifies performance expectancy as the strongest determinant of technology adoption ( Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). The present study extends this evidence to Generative AI within a Ghanaian higher-education context, suggesting that students primarily consider the perceived educational value of GenAI when forming their intention to use it. This reinforces the argument that students evaluate AI according to its educational value and contribution to learning outcomes. Regarding language learning, Matthews (2024) argued that interaction becomes more fluid for students who view AI as a cognitive partner that assists with outlines or syntax. Furthermore, the significant positive association of Effort Expectancy suggests that the nature of the interaction is defined by its accessibility. The natural language processing (NLP) abilities of large language models allow for a plug-and-play experience that is far simpler than traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS), which often require technical training ( Karahan and Bilgili, 2025 ). Furthermore, the significant positive association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention suggests that perceived ease of interaction is relevant to students’ intention to use GenAI. The natural-language interface of many GenAI systems may make interaction more accessible than technologies requiring greater technical familiarity. However, the present study did not directly compare GenAI with other educational technologies. Contrary to the original UTAUT model, Social Influence was not significantly associated with Behavioral Intention. This finding suggests that Social Influence did not explain additional variation in students’ intention to use GenAI after the other predictors in the model were considered. The finding differs from the traditional UTAUT proposition that social influence contributes to technology acceptance ( Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). However, the present study did not examine the specific social circumstances surrounding students’ GenAI use. Therefore, the reason for the non-significant relationship cannot be established from the present data. Future research could examine how lecturer expectations, peer influence, institutional norms, and students’ patterns of GenAI use may help explain the role of Social Influence in GenAI acceptance. A key finding of this study was the significant negative association between Digital Learning Anxiety and students’ intention to use Generative AI (H5). Effort Expectancy was also negatively associated with Digital Learning Anxiety (H4), indicating that students who perceived GenAI as easier to use tended to report lower levels of anxiety. These findings are consistent with Karal and Özdemir (2025) and Kristandl (2025) , who identified AI-related anxiety as relevant to students’ engagement with Generative AI. However, the cross-sectional nature of the present data does not establish the direction or causal nature of these relationships. The mediation analysis showed that lower Effort Expectancy was associated with higher Digital Learning Anxiety, while higher Digital Learning Anxiety was associated with lower Behavioral Intention. The indirect association was statistically significant but small; however, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering or causality among these variables. The findings contribute to research on GenAI acceptance by showing that affective responses may be considered alongside traditional UTAUT constructs. Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy were positively associated with Behavioral Intention, whereas Digital Learning Anxiety was negatively associated with Behavioral Intention. Social Influence, however, did not explain additional variation in Behavioral Intention within the specified structural model. These findings suggest that models of GenAI acceptance may benefit from considering students’ affective responses alongside their evaluations of usefulness and ease of use. The significant indirect association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention through Digital Learning Anxiety also provides evidence for examining affective processes alongside UTAUT predictors. However, this indirect association was small, accounting for approximately 11% of the total association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention. Most of the association was therefore direct. Moreover, because the variables were measured at the same point in time, the indirect association should not be interpreted as evidence that Effort Expectancy causes changes in Digital Learning Anxiety or that anxiety subsequently causes changes in Behavioral Intention. The findings suggest some practical considerations that may be examined further in the design of GenAI-supported learning environments. Given the positive association between Performance Expectancy and Behavioral Intention, universities may consider helping students understand the potential academic uses and limitations of GenAI. Similarly, the associations involving Effort Expectancy and Digital Learning Anxiety suggest that accessible guidance and opportunities to become familiar with GenAI may be worth investigating as possible ways of supporting students’ engagement with these technologies. Universities may also consider providing low-stakes opportunities in which students can explore appropriate uses of GenAI and receive guidance on academic integrity and responsible use. However, the present cross-sectional findings do not demonstrate that such interventions will increase GenAI adoption or reduce anxiety. These suggestions should therefore be treated as design hypotheses that require evaluation through experimental, longitudinal, or intervention-based research. This study
analysis.limitations: Despite its contributions, this study has several limitations. First, the cross-sectional design does not permit the establishment of long-term causal relationships. Because Effort Expectancy, Digital Learning Anxiety, and Behavioral Intention were measured at the same point in time, the indirect relationship identified in the model does not establish temporal or causal mediation. Reverse relationships and unmeasured factors that may influence these constructs cannot be ruled out. Accordingly, the observed indirect association may also reflect alternative directional relationships or common causes that were not included in the model. Additionally, because all measures were collected using self-reported responses, the findings may be influenced by respondents’ subjective perceptions. Although statistical procedures were employed to assess the validity and reliability of the measurement model, future studies may benefit from combining survey data with behavioral or observational measures of AI usage. The use of convenience sampling also limits the representativeness of the sample. Because participants were recruited during scheduled lecture sessions, students who were absent during data collection were less likely to be represented. The findings should therefore not be generalized to all university students in Ghana without caution. The structural model did not include potential control variables such as gender, university level, prior GenAI experience, device access, or English proficiency. Some of these factors may be associated with students’ perceptions of GenAI, Digital Learning Anxiety, and Behavioral Intention. Consequently, the observed relationships may partly reflect unmeasured confounding, and future studies should examine the robustness of these associations after accounting for relevant demographic, technological, and language-related characteristics. Although the study was conducted among university students in an English-medium academic setting and the questionnaire included items contextualized to language-related academic activities, English proficiency and L2-specific psychological constructs were not directly measured. The findings should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that the observed relationships are specifically attributable to students’ English proficiency or L2-related anxiety. Again, the rapidly evolving nature of generative AI limits the temporal stability of the findings. By targeting humanities students in one academic setting, it becomes difficult to establish the effectiveness in other disciplines, such as STEM. Moreover, the convenience sampling approach may have introduced selection bias because participation depended on students’ availability and willingness to respond. Finally, the quantitative design did not permit an in-depth exploration of students’ lived experiences when interacting with Generative AI. Future qualitative studies could provide richer insights into these experiences. Future studies could extend the framework by examining additional factors such as Academic Integrity Awareness and investigating whether the observed relationships differ across academic disciplines. Longitudinal research could examine how students’ AI-related anxiety and acceptance change as their experience with GenAI develops over time. Qualitative research may also provide deeper insight into the social and institutional factors associated with students’ decisions to use GenAI. Finally, empirical studies examining the effects of GenAI-supported learning on students’ actual academic performance and AI-use behaviour would provide a more balanced understanding of its educational implications. items.title: Where Do We Look? Visual Attention Competition Between Hyper-Salient Objects and AI-Generated Virtual Endorsers in Generative Artificial Intelligence Advertising

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) advertising, defined as advertising content created or substantially assisted by generative AI systems (AIGC), has introduced new visual features that combine algorithmically generated objects with human-like representations. Hyper-salient objects, defined by exaggerated perceptual prominence and semantic incongruity, and AI-generated virtual endorsers, represented by human-like AI-created figures, have become increasingly common in such advertisements. However, little is known about how these distinct visual cues compete for consumers’ limited attentional resources when presented together. Drawing on visual attention and scene perception perspectives, this study investigated how hyper-salient objects and AI-generated virtual endorsers influence visual attention allocation in AI-generated advertising. A 2 (hyper-salient object: present vs. absent) × 2 (AI endorser: present vs. absent) between-subjects eye-tracking experiment was conducted with 160 participants in a controlled laboratory setting using static AI-generated advertisements. Eye movements were recorded, and memory was assessed using signal detection measures (d′) from a recognition task involving target and distractor advertisements. Advertising attitude and product trust were measured using established scales. Results from linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models showed that hyper-salient objects increased early fixation probability and attracted a larger dwell time proportion, demonstrating strong attentional capture. AI-generated endorsers also attracted attention when presented alone, but their proportional attention share decreased when hyper-salient objects were simultaneously present. The effects of these visual elements on memory and product trust were conditional on their co-occurrence rather than uniform across conditions. Within the specific set of experimentally constructed stimuli and four sampled product categories, this research contributes to AIGC advertising literature by developing a visual competition perspective on how multiple AI-generated visual cues interact under limited attentional capacity, offering implications for designing effective generative AI advertisements.

items.abstract_text: Abstract Purpose The primary objective of the study was to determine how clinically accurate and useful ChatGPT-4o–generated outputs are when identical prompts are entered simultaneously in 3 independent ChatGPT sessions utilizing the same user-facing model. The secondary objective was to identify whether differences in outputs affect clinical outcomes (ie, impact variability). Methods Five clinical prompts focusing on diabetes management and counseling were developed. Each clinical prompt was simultaneously inputted into 3 separate devices using ChatGPT-4o to generate outputs. Through a modified Delphi technique, 5 clinical pharmacy faculty members with expertise in diabetes management independently rated each ChatGPT-generated output for accuracy (poor, borderline, or good) usefulness (not useful, somewhat useful, or very useful) and impact variability (low, moderate, or high). After initial assessment, responses were collated and anonymously shared among the pharmacy faculty raters. The faculty members were invited to revise their evaluations based on collective feedback, then convened in a virtual panel with moderators to discuss evaluations and work towards consensus. Results Consensus was achieved for all ChatGPT outputs. Accuracy ratings ranged from borderline to good. Two of the clinical prompts yielded outputs that received different accuracy ratings, which may have impacted variability. Usefulness ratings ranged from somewhat useful to very useful, with one clinical prompt yielding outputs that received different usefulness ratings. Conclusion While ChatGPT-4o outputs were generally accurate and useful, limitations and inconsistencies were noted. Users should be aware simultaneously generated outputs across multiple devices using ChatGPT can vary in their accuracy and usefulness in diabetes management.

items.abstract_text: ABSTRACT Informatics education requires instructional designs that connect conceptual understanding with procedural application and contextual problem-solving. This study aimed to develop an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-integrated course based on Problem-Based Learning (PBL) to support these two competencies among junior high school students. The product was developed using the Moodle platform by combining digital learning materials, problem-based activities, and AI support in the form of explanations and learning-material summaries. The needs analysis involved 113 students, while the learning-outcome evaluation employed an experimental group and a control group, each consisting of 34 students, using pretests and posttests. The needs analysis revealed percentages of 23% for decomposition, 50% for pattern recognition, 35% for abstraction, and 44% for algorithms. In procedural application of computational thinking, the experimental group's mean score increased from 58.40 to 82.60, whereas the control group's mean score increased from 57.90 to 70.30. For contextual problem-solving, the experimental group's mean score increased from 56.80 to 83.10, while the control group's mean score rose from 57.20 to 71.40. Descriptively, the experimental group demonstrated greater improvement in both measured competencies. These findings indicate the potential of the developed AI-integrated PBL course to support Informatics learning; however, its statistical effectiveness must be confirmed through inferential testing. items.abstract_text: Kajian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis bagaimana cognitive offloading melalui penggunaan generative AI (GenAI) dapat memengaruhi cognitive empowerment dan mengidentifikasi peran literasi AI dalam proses tersebut. Permasalahan kajian ini berfokus pada bagaimana pengalihan beban kognitif kepada AI memengaruhi kapasitas belajar mahasiswa dan bagaimana kemampuan literasi AI oleh mahasiswa dapat mencegah berkembangnya ketergantungan kognitif. Metode yang digunakan adalah kajian konseptual melalui telaah literatur integratif terhadap literatur mengenai cognitive offloading, literasi AI, GenAI, metakognisi, dan pembelajaran mandiri. Hasil kajian ini menunjukkan bahwa cognitive offloading tidak secara langsung memberikan sifat negatif, namun terdapat konsekuensi dalam ketergantungan pada tingkat kendali dan keterlibatan kognitif mahasiswa. Literasi AI berperan sebagai kompetensi pengarah melalui kemampuan memahami keterbatasan AI, menggunakan AI secara strategis, mengevaluasi keluaran, mengatur tingkat ketergantungan, dan melakukan refleksi terhadap proses belajar. Kajian ini menegaskan bahwa penggunaan GenAI dapat bergeser dari pengurangan beban berpikir menuju penguatan kapasitas belajar apabila mahasiswa tetap mempertahankan cognitive agency dalam proses pembelajaran.

items.abstract_text: The evolution of digital media and the convergence of multiple platforms have profoundly influenced adolescent behaviour and cognitive functioning. This study examined the impact of media convergence on the behaviour and attention span of adolescents in selected secondary schools in Rivers State, Nigeria. Employing a survey research design, data were collected from 330 students across three secondary schools using structured questionnaires and teacher interviews. Findings indicate that 60% of respondents reported high daily exposure to online media, with the majority acknowledging that media use affects focus, reduces study time, and influences classroom behaviour. The results highlight a significant relationship between prolonged media exposure and decreased attention span, increased distractibility, and altered behavioural patterns. The study concludes that while digital media can enhance learning opportunities, excessive exposure poses risks to adolescents’ cognitive development and academic performance. Recommendations include strengthening digital literacy education, implementing screen-time regulations, and promoting balanced media use in schools. The findings provide valuable insights for educators, parents, and policymakers seeking to mitigate the adverse effects of media convergence on adolescents.

By relying on short-horizon feedback, this approach ignores the profound, longitudinal externalities of persistent human-AI interaction, which can lead to adverse outcomes such as cognitive atrophy, social erosion, and diminished human agency.
