publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: Introduction South Africa is moving towards AI-based digital border management, including biometric screening, drone-supported aerial surveillance and the Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) system. This paper explores the educational consequences of that shift, with a special focus on the civic digital literacy that algorithmic immigration governance requires of citizens, policymakers and educators. Methods The study takes a qualitative, interpretive approach, drawing on critical digital pedagogy, algorithmic accountability theory and postcolonial education studies. It synthesises peer-reviewed scholarly works, policy documents and grey literature on the Border Management Authority's use of biometric surveillance, drone technology and the ETA system. A corpus of 53 sources was screened through an adapted PRISMA-style procedure and analysed through a three-phase thematic synthesis that produced five descriptive and three analytical themes. Results AI-based border governance exposes a pressing and largely ignored digital literacy gap. The communities most affected by algorithmic immigration decisions are those without the conceptual tools to engage with, debate or take part in the governance of the AI systems that regulate their lives and rights. Standard digital literacy programmes are not sufficient to equip learners with the knowledge to participate in the governance of algorithmically driven systems. Discussion Geography and social sciences education has a special role in equipping learners with the skills needed for critical AI citizenship. The study proposes that algorithmic governance be incorporated into the school curriculum, that community-facing digital civic education programmes be developed, and that participatory AI accountability structures be established in border management. The study advances digital learning innovation by theorising civic AI literacy as a new educational priority in the Global South and by showing that algorithmic governance necessitates a fundamental redefinition of digital citizenship education.

analysis.methods: The research approach of this project is qualitative and interpretive. The way used involves a critical documentary analysis as well as a systematic literature review. Since the study focuses on interpreting the meanings, power relations and educational ramifications that are inherent in South African AI border governance systems and in relevant literatures on digital literacy, algorithmic accountability, and civic education, an interpretive model, which supports this aim, is chosen. But quantitative research would be suitable to form continuous of adoption or testing causal hypotheses (Creswell and Poth, 2018) . Critical documentary analysis method, guided by the study's theoretical perspectives, is a way of critically reading and challenging the epistemological assumptions and governance logics that are embedded in policy documents as well as in the AI governance systems that these documents portray (Bowen, 2009) . The systematic literature review is a research method to locate, evaluate and synthesise relevant and available research around the topic of the research. This method is used here to map out, select and integrate the research literature on digital literacy, algorithmic governance and civic education (Tranfield et al. 2003) . The data were collected from three main categories of sources: (i) policy and governance documents, parliamentary responses, BMA operational reports, Department of Home Affairs strategic and annual reports, and government press releases related to the ETA system and digital border management strategy for 2022 to 2026; (ii) peer-reviewed literature on digital literacy, algorithmic governance, civic education, and AI ethics, obtained through structured searches of Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Education Resources Information Centre (ERIC) database. Some of the search terms used are algorithmic governance AND civic education; digital literacy AND AI governance; critical digital pedagogy AND citizenship; immigration AND artificial intelligence AND rights; postcolonial education AND digital technology; and AI border management AND human rights. (iii) grey literature from illustrious institutions like the South African Human Rights Commission and the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, was used. Table 1 details the sources searched, the search strings in Boolean form and the limits applied. Terms within each string were combined using the Boolean operator AND, and the strings were submitted as separate searches whose results were pooled (equivalent to combining the strings with OR). Peer-reviewed and grey literature were limited between 2015 and 2026 and policy and governance documents between 2022 and 2026. Policy and governance documents were retrieved from the official portals of the Border Management Authority, the Department of Home Affairs and the South African Parliament and replies by the Minister of Home Affairs to parliamentary questions from the Parliamentary Monitoring Group (PMG) website, which publishes them. Grey literature was sourced from the publications of the South African Human Rights Commission (SAHRC) and the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR). The sources and their bibliographic details were last checked on 10 October 2026. Relying on published policy documents and scholarly literature means that the study reflects what institutions and scholars say about AI border governance rather than how such systems operate in practice or impact those subject to them. Policy texts report intentions and capabilities but may omit operational practice. The parliamentary replies relied on for the South African border systems describe aerial surveillance, biometric verification and pre-arrival risk screening but do not state the algorithmic methods or criteria used and so the classification of these systems as AI-enabled in this paper is the author's analytical judgement not a finding reported by the replies. Figure 1 reports the stages and criteria of screening but not the number of records at each intermediate stage, so that readers cannot reconstruct the yield of the searches. The corpus was limited to publicly available sources with full text, the coding was interpretive and was conducted by one researcher with no independent second coder, and the themes in Table 3 should therefore be read as a transparent interpretive account and as propositions to be tested rather than as findings that generalise across the corpus. Besides the three directions of future work already mentioned, there are two more. Firstly, getting primary data by doing empirical fieldwork in border communities and schools as well as qualitative interviews with student's teachers community members, and immigration officials will be necessary for testing the theoretical structure presented in this paper against real-life situations. Secondly, civic AI literacy learning materials codesigned with geography and social sciences teachers, students, and border community representatives through participatory curriculum development projects would generate new educational materials tailored to the environment of the communities most affected by algorithmic border governance. Third, case studies on civic AI literacy educational strategies addressing AI border governance in other southern African nations like Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Botswana that share borders with South Africa and are influenced by its border management systems, will provide the regional angle that is required for a full understanding of the educational aspects of AI-driven border governance in the southern African setting. Future empirical research. Empirical field investigation is the most important next step. Interviews with Geography and Social Sciences educators, with border officials, and with migrants and members of border communities would show how algorithmic decisions are experienced and contested, and whether the five literacy demands in DT3 match the needs that people themselves describe. Such work would require institutional ethical clearance and particular care in working with migrants, for whom participation may carry legal and personal risks.

This explains the paper's focus on teacher education and on the disciplinary function of Geography and Social Sciences and might have made the educational implications of AI border governance more salient to the author than its technical or security aspects. The author attempted to mitigate this by anchoring the coding in three explicit theoretical perspectives and by describing in detail the search, selection and coding steps as presented in Tables 1 to 3 and Figure 1 , thus allowing readers to assess the derivation of the themes and to judge them for themselves. This paper has limitation points that need to be addressed. Firstly, the documentary research method used which based on the published secondary sources and public policy documentation cannot completely capture the border community's immigration officials, educators, or students' experiences who are experiencing the emerging AI border governance theoretically and practically. That is because the study does not have primary qualitative data from these stakeholders, which is a big methodological limitation that future research must address. Secondly, the research depends on publicly available policy documents which probably will not reveal the real operational sides of the AI system, the informal governance practices that determine how algorithmic decisions are implemented and the technical specifications of the ETA and BMA systems that are kept confidential in public documents. Since AI technology is constantly changing, the capabilities and limitations of the technology pointed out in the literature reviewed could be a bit different over the period during which South Africa's digital border management systems are being rolled out. The ETA system Really was still in the process of being rolled out at the time of writing, and the real design, data sources, and algorithmic logic of the system might be different from those described in the existing policy documents. Because of this, detailed research of the implementation and operationalisation of AI border governance systems in South Africa is a must for producing an empirically based knowledge base that can be used to inform educational and policy developments.

items.title: INTEGRATION OF GENERATIVE AI SKILLS IN JOB REQUIREMENTS: EVIDENCE FROM JOB ADVERTISEMENTS IN GEORGIA

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

items.abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools has created a demand for new skills in labour markets. However, research into how employers articulate GenAI competencies in job advertisements has focused almost exclusively on large, technologically advanced economies. This study examines how employers in Georgia, a small upper-middle-income transitional economy, indicate GenAI skill requirements in job advertisements, considering four dimensions: skill visibility, linguistic framing, organisational readiness and skill depth. Deductive content analysis was applied to 94 job advertisements collected in January 2026 from three major Georgian labour market platforms (LinkedIn, Jobs.ge and HR.ge). Each advertisement was coded using a structured 20-indicator codebook derived from established theoretical frameworks. The results show that employers articulate GenAI skills in two ways: by explicitly naming the tool, which is present in 38.3 per cent of advertisements, and by using implicit task language, which is present in 61.7 per cent of advertisements and constitutes the dominant form of signalling. Regardless of occupation or skill depth, employers frame GenAI requirements as mandatory in 81.9 per cent of advertisements, indicating the rapid institutionalisation of GenAI literacy as a baseline labour market expectation. Signals of organisational readiness remain weak: only 21.3 per cent of job advertisements acknowledge any organisational role in enabling AI adoption, while the remaining 78.7 per cent present GenAI competence purely as a prerequisite for candidates. Skill complexity is almost evenly divided between basic and advanced requirements, and occupation strongly predicts this division, creating a clear distinction between a technically advanced group and a large group adopting AI on a more general operational level. analysis.methods: This study primarily employs a deductive content analysis of job advertisements. Content analysis of job advertisements is a well-established way of inferring latent skill demand structures from texts generated by employers. Deductive coding based on a theoryderived codebook enables the systematic and replicable classification of skill signals across a body of work. Job advertisements were collected from three major Georgian-language and bilingual online labor market platforms: LinkedIn, Jobs.ge and HR.ge. Data collection was conducted in January 2026. An initial corpus was assembled by searching each platform using a predefined set of GenAI-related keywords, including but not limited to: artificial intelligence, generative AI, ChatGPT, LLM, large language model, prompt engineering, AI tools and machine learning. Searches were conducted in both Georgian and English to capture the full range of postings in the bilingual labor market. Advertisements were filtered based on the ISCO-08 occupational classification to include only roles where GenAI exposure was theoretically plausible. Of these, 94 advertisements containing at least one identifiable GenAI competency signal were selected for analysis. A structured codebook comprising 20 binary and categorical indicators was developed across four analytical dimensions that correspond to the four research questions: (1) explicit vs. implicit GenAI skill signaling; (2) mandatory vs. preferred framing and description granularity; (3) organizational tone, training support and readiness communication; and (4) skill complexity level and specific task types. The full codebook is presented in Table 1 . Limitations. The sample is drawn from advertisements that already contain GenAI signals, which precludes any inference about the broader population of postings. The cross-sectional design also prevents the framing lifecycle from being traced over time. The moderate sample size (n = 94) restricts the ability to conduct in-depth or subgroup analyses. Furthermore, job advertisement text may not perfectly correspond to actual workplace AI practices due to its reflection of employer communication norms and competitive signalling strategies.
analysis.discussion: The following section provides an analytical discussion of the study's findings regarding the integration of Vol. 12 No. 5, 2026 generative AI in the Georgian labour market. Across job advertisements, GenAI requirements tend to be expressed in broad and non-specific terms, with little operational detail regarding the expected level of competence, the required tools, or specific applications. This reflects a general demand for ' AI capability' rather than specific technical or task-level expectations. In this context, the prevalence of implicit task language over explicit tool naming further emphasises that employers are primarily signalling a general expectation of AIenabled work practices rather than specifying precise technological skills or platforms. Consequently, GenAI competence is perceived as a flexible, cross-functional requirement rather than a structured, measurable skill set. Signals of organisational readiness remain notably weak. While organisations project enthusiasm for AI adoption and use a positive tone, the majority present GenAI competence as a prerequisite that is already in place. Only a small proportion of advertisements acknowledge any organisational role in enabling AI capability. Firms express their intention to adopt without providing the structural accompaniments -training, infrastructure, governance frameworks and tool accessthat characterise genuine organisational readiness. The near-total absence of certification requirements exacerbates this issue. When employers do not specify how competence should be demonstrated or provide pathways for its development, candidates are left to their own devices, resulting in AI competence becoming a tacit and socially stratified credential that favours those with access to informal learning resources. There are two clear segments of GenAI labour demand. The sharp occupational bifurcation in skill depth lends support to this model. The technical depth segment (Systems Architects, AI/ML Engineers and Software Developers) requires advanced competencies and specifies tools explicitly. This segment is concentrated in remote roles and shows a higher level of training provision. In contrast, the operational adoption segment (Designers, Marketers, Project Managers and Content Creators) requires basic workflow integration and uses implicit framing. This segment is predominantly office-based and shows nearzero training support. This study is the first to provide a systematic analysis of GenAI skill demand as expressed in job advertisements in the Georgian labour market. Four key findings emerge. Firstly, GenAI competence has become a general labour market expectation, regardless of skill depth, across occupations. Secondly, the dominant mode of articulation is implicit -workflow integration language without specific tool naming -meaning that functional AI expectations exceed those revealed by explicit mentions. Thirdly, signals of organisational readiness are weak: employers express enthusiasm for AI while presenting competence as a prerequisite for candidates, with fewer than one in five advertisements acknowledging training provision. Fourthly, the demand for skill depth is sharply stratified by occupation, dividing the market into segments characterised by either broad operational adoption or technical depth. The following evidence-based recommendations address the distinct needs of policy, practice, and research. With regard to workforce development policy, the discrepancy between the widespread mandatory requirement for AI competence and the minimal provision of training indicates a systemic market failure. If AI proficiency is universally required but there is no institutional pathway to it or funding for it, the supply will lag behind the demand, resulting in widening labour market inequalities. For educators, the dominance of implicit framing means that AI literacy programmes must address functional integration skills across a wide range of occupations. As for researchers, the Georgian case shows that the institutionalisation of GenAI in the labour market can happen quickly in smaller transitional economies. This calls for broader cross-national comparative analyses. Future research should build on this analysis by examining the gap between advertised requirements and actual workplace AI practices, and investigating whether the organisational readiness deficit observed here reflects a temporary adoption lag or a permanent structural feature of smaller labour markets. items.abstract_text: Purpose In the AI era, digital transformation has become essential for enterprises to adapt as complex systems to uncertain business environments. In this work, we aim to analyze the evolutionary dynamics of AI-driven enterprise digital transformation (EDT), focusing on its evolution and impact on enterprise performance from a system cybernetics perspective. Design/methodology/approach We employ evolutionary dynamics analysis grounded in game theory to model the EDT process, and perform an econometric and empirical analysis on a sample of Chinese A-share-listed enterprises from 2009 to 2023. The approach encompasses heterogeneity analysis, moderation effect models, such as testing enterprise environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors and market concentration, and threshold effect analyses. Findings The evolutionary dynamics analysis finds that increasing the risk-averse benefits of traditional enterprises and reducing the additional benefit coefficient would hinder EDT. Increasing the investment of technology enterprises in internal resource restructuring accelerates the transformation process. Empirically, AI significantly contributes to EDT. ESG positively moderates the relationship between AI and EDT, while market concentration exerts a negative moderating effect. Furthermore, AI and EDT show an inverted U-shaped trend when R&D intensity exceeds a specific threshold, while a U-shaped trend is observed when enterprise performance exceeds a specific threshold. Originality/value In this work, we uncover the complex, non-linear cybernetic feedback loops, such as U-shaped and inverted U-shaped, and boundary conditions, such as ESG and market concentration for AI-driven EDT, offering systemic strategies for enterprises adapting to the digital ecosystem.

items.abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) commonly employ key–value (KV) caching to avoid recomputing previous attention states during autoregressive inference. However, its measured performance benefit depends on workload characteristics and the memory environment. This study presents a controlled systems characterization across input context length, model-specific grouped-query attention configurations, and GPU-memory residency. Experiments use Qwen2.5-3B and SmolLM3-3B under verified fully resident conditions with fixed 128-token generation, prompt lengths from 128 to 2048 tokens, randomized cache-enabled/cache-disabled execution, GPU telemetry, and repeated paired validation. End-to-end generation speedup increases from 1.34× to 8.31× for Qwen2.5-3B and from 1.28× to 8.62× for SmolLM3-3B. At 2048 prompt tokens, 30 randomized paired trials confirm mean speedups of 8.10× and 8.51×, corresponding to runtime reductions of 87.65% and 88.25%, while physical GPU-memory utilization remains below 61%. SmolLM3-3B requires twice the theoretical KV-cache storage per token, yet both models show comparable context-dependent scaling in the fully resident regime. Because the models differ in characteristics beyond KV-head count, this cross-model comparison is descriptive and does not attribute the observed performance difference causally to GQA configuration. A separate Mistral-7B case study shows that apparent end-to-end speedup changes substantially under memory pressure; the underlying memory-system mechanism is not isolated. These results establish cache-related end-to-end generation speedup as workload- and system-dependent and demonstrate that meaningful benchmarking requires reporting context length, cache configuration, model and cache footprints, physical accelerator-memory residency, runtime, throughput, and relevant GPU-memory conditions during each inference experiment.

items.abstract_text: Edge AI deployment requires low-latency inference on devices with tight constraints in size, weight, power, and cost. NVIDIA TensorRT accelerates inference through layer fusion, precision reduction, and kernel auto-tuning, but a model containing even one unsupported operator cannot be compiled into a single engine. This paper presents a hybrid TensorRT–PyTorch deployment in which the supported subnetworks run as TensorRT engines while the unsupported operations fall back to native PyTorch, and applies it to an attention-based convolutional neural network (ACNN) whose region-of-interest sampling operators are unsupported. On an NVIDIA Jetson Nano, the hybrid approach reduced the end-to-end latency of ACNN-dsc, the fastest native PyTorch model, from 38.37 ms to 20.40 ms (1.88×) under FP32. Under FP16, the hybrid ACNN-k3 achieved the lowest latency of 17.78 ms, a 2.23× speedup over its PyTorch FP32 counterpart and 2.16× over the fastest PyTorch model. Stepwise profiling of the image preprocessing pipeline showed that transferring raw images and performing most conversions on the GPU more than halves preprocessing latency. Further analyses across devices, precisions, and frameworks show that practical latency on edge AI accelerators depends on hardware and runtime factors beyond FLOPs and model size.

items.abstract_text: Despite substantial investments in artificial intelligence (AI) training, logistics organizations often struggle to translate these investments into measurable improvements in employee performance. Drawing on the extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Cognitive Load Theory, and Distributed Cognition Theory, this study examines how three AI-TPACK training dimensions—Strategic, Generative, and Optimization AI Training—are associated with employees’ innovative behavior through cognitive (Task–Technology Fit, AI Self-Efficacy) and affective (Perceived Technology Attractiveness, AI Usage Intention) mechanisms. Survey data from 245 logistics practitioners (cross-sectional, single-source) were analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis, competing structural models, and bootstrapped indirect effects in a final integrated model. The originally proposed dual-track structure was not supported; the data favored a cross-linked specification in which cognitive beliefs inform attitudes across tracks and attractiveness precedes usage intention. Strategic AI training was associated with innovative behavior indirectly, Generative AI training both directly and indirectly, and Optimization AI training showed no unique association once the other dimensions were controlled. Neither Training Environment Quality nor Supervisor Support Leadership moderated the hypothesized relationships in a robust way, although both showed direct associations with outcomes (Training Environment Quality with Task–Technology Fit, β = 0.288; Supervisor Support with innovative behavior, β = 0.141). These cross-sectional, single-source associations refine the technology acceptance literature for AI training and inform HRD strategies for digital transformation in logistics.

items.abstract_text: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/Å; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.

Periodic systems additionally require a treatment of wrapped coordinates and periodic images that is outside the evaluated formulation. Conservative forces follow from differentiating the model energy at differentiable configurations. This construction is useful for keeping energy and force predictions consistent, but it does not establish the accuracy of molecular dynamics trajectories or smoothness at every configuration. A node exactly at the centroid, changes in the neighbor graph, and the numerical floors in the feature map deserve attention when the mechanism is used in a simulator. Such considerations are properties of the implementation and representation, independent of the reported validation errors. The experiments establish improved energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters with one backbone family. Aggregate errors do not isolate the contribution of a particular interaction distance or identify a learned electrostatic or dispersion component. The scalar interface permits integration into other geometric models, but performance in other domains has not been established here. RKA combines centroid-based radial features with content-dependent attention to exchange information beyond local graph connectivity. items.abstract_text: When students use generative AI to produce their work, the learning process becomes invisible. Established frameworks such as Bloom's taxonomy then classify the cognitive level of what the AI produced, not what the student contributed. We propose the Human Agency Depth Taxonomy (HADT), a preliminary six-tier taxonomy that classifies the engineering contribution a student makes in a prompt, independent of the AI's output. HADT combines three dimensions: contextual bandwidth, engineering abstraction and student agency. We applied HADT to 962 prompts from 105 students' structured AI Journals in an AI-permissive, first-year software engineering course of 145 students, and examined how agency changed over ten journalled weeks. Most prompts (84.2%) carried some student contribution beyond delegation.

items.abstract_text: Subject of Research. This study focuses on the digital banking landscape and the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in private banking and wealth management in Switzerland. More specifically, it examines how technological innovations – ranging from process automation and generative AI to advanced data analytics – alter the operational dynamics, customer relations, and structural competitiveness of Swiss private banks in the context of shifting client expectations and rigorous regulatory environments. Methodology. The research employs a qualitative analytical research design that uses triangulation of secondary evidence. It systematically integrates and cross-checks academic literature on digital finance, fintech adoption and robo-advisory trust, alongside empirical data, regulatory frameworks and market insights from reputable Swiss and international organisations. The primary data sources analysed were supervisory guides from the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA), reports from the Swiss Bankers Association, digital maturity benchmarks from Deloitte Switzerland and private banking market profitability assessments from KPMG and PwC Switzerland. Purpose. The main objective of this paper is to provide a comprehensive assessment of the impact of digital transformation and the deployment of AI on the traditional Swiss private banking model. By analysing seven key dimensions – technological progress, customer expectations, process optimization, data analytics, risk and security, regulation/compliance, and market trajectories – the study aims to clarify the economic mechanisms driving digital adaptation, identify the structural barriers preventing rapid technology adoption, and evaluate the strategic options available to Swiss banks facing intense global competition and margin compression. Findings and Conclusion. The study reveals a significant discrepancy between Switzerland's position as a global leader in asset management, with CHF 9.3 trillion under management, and its digital banking maturity score of 39 out of 60. Although private banking clients continue to establish relationships based on traditional factors such as reputation, trust and personal referrals, they are also demanding friction-free digital execution, personalised dashboards and virtual investment simulations. AI has been proven to have high economic value when acting as a productivity layer centred around advisors, optimising processes such as client onboarding, document extraction, compliance screening and portfolio monitoring. However, it is not as effective when acting as an autonomous replacement for human relationship managers. Ultimately, the integration of digital banking and AI is causing a clear market polarisation. Large-scale institutions are successfully absorbing the substantial fixed costs associated with technology, data governance and regulatory compliance under the frameworks of FINMA and the European Union (such as DORA and the EU AI Act). Conversely, smaller Swiss private banks are under severe pressure to increase their profitability and consolidate, unless they adopt highly focused niche advisory models. The paper therefore concludes that urgent regulatory attention and strategic repositioning are necessary to preserve the overall image and international attractiveness of the Swiss private banking ecosystem.

items.abstract_text: This study examined the extent to which senior high school teachers monitor AI-generated written outputs, focusing on the use of AI detectors, manual review, and cross-checking results. The study respondents were teachers from the Humanities and Social Sciences (HUMSS) strand of Philippine Christian University-Dasmariñas. The researchers collected data through a structured questionnaire and analyzed it using descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation. Results showed that teachers used AI detectors and cross-checking to a moderate extent, while they used manual review to a high extent and found it significant. Teachers faced challenges such as limitations in AI detection tools and time constraints in manual evaluation and cross-checking. These findings highlight the importance of a layered monitoring approach, where teacher judgment remains central, and AI tools serve as supplementary aids. The study provides evidence for developing clear guidelines and practices that balance ethical assessment, professional discretion, and responsible integration of AI in student writing evaluation. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, AI-generated text, teacher monitoring strategies, manual review, cross-checking

items.abstract_text: Today, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is quickly becoming a staple of university students' work, as it can provide instant answers to information search, writing, explanation and problem solving. While GenAI can aid in learning, overreliance can lessen students' independent thinking. This study explores the ties between generative AI reliance and students' problem-solving skills, focusing on cognitive offloading as a mediation factor and AI literacy as a moderation factor. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design is suggested with a sample of 100 University students. The data will be analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, regression, mediation and moderation analysis through SPSS. The conceptual model suggests that students' problem-solving ability may be linked to their degree of cognitive offloading, which could be further linked to their reliance on GenAI. The authors suggest AI literacy as a boundary condition that could affect the relationship between GenAI dependence and problem solving ability. New studies suggest that students' use of GenAI in problem-solving is multi-layered and constructive, as well as thoughtless, and that there are four aspects of AI literacy: knowledge, application, evaluation, and understanding of ethical issues. Thus, the present study is centered on not only students' usage of GenAI, but also how reliance on GenAI can impact their thinking processes when addressing academic challenges.

analysis.discussion: The model presented here serves as a response to an educational psychology question: Does the dependence on GenAI change the way that cognitive tasks are performed in such a way as to impact students' problem-solving ability?The illustrative results indicate an increasing correlation between the reliance on GenAI and cognitive offloading with increasing dependence on GenAI. This is in line with the theoretical model of cognitive offloading which posits that people rely on external resources to offload their internal cognition (Risko & Gilbert, 2016) . In the case of GenAI, the external resource is significantly more powerful than traditional resources in that it can create explanations, arguments, examples and even full solutions.The hypothesized negative correlation between GenAI dependence and problem solving ability is also aligned with recent concerns with technology dependence and independent learning. A complicated relationship between GenAI use, perceived efficiency, confidence, and dependence with technology was revealed by Zhang & Xu (2025) .However, the literature does not lead one to believe that GenAI itself is harmful. According to the evidence-based assessment, the positive effects of GenAI on student learning and higher-order thinking within the classroom are closely associated with the proper adoption of GenAI tools (Chen & Cheung, 2025; Liu et al., 2025) .What is important is then the difference between dependence and purposeful usage. Multiple patterns of using GenAI for problem solving were illustrated in the article by Hou et al. (2025) , suggesting that this reliance is not necessarily a problem; therefore, one should not assume that any student's use of GenAI for problem-solving is problematic. Another crucial explanation to consider is AI literacy. If students grasp the functionality of GenAI, the limitations of GenAI, the evaluation of the outputs, and the responsible use of GenAI, they may be less likely to give up their thinking skills to GenAI. Evaluation and responsible use are recurring themes that have been consistently highlighted as core aspects of AI and GenAI literacy in recent literature (Lintner, 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Park, 2025) .So, the educational task is not just about minimizing the students' use of GenAI. Rather, universities need to introduce students to using GenAI, but not transfer ownership of the thinking process to the technology. The learning potential of generative AI is newly available for universities, but it is highly reliant on how students use it. The present study suggests that overreliance on GenAI might have a relationship with student problem-solving ability via the cognitive offloading pathway and that AI literacy could affect the strength of this relationship. This is the key innovation of the model, as it asks a much more complex question of whether students use GenAI or not. Instead, it investigates how reliance on GenAI could alter students' thinking processes and if there is a way for students to have a way to remain independent in problem-solving with the support of AI literacy. The study thus offers a specific educational psychology approach for studying GenAI dependence in university education, as well as cognitive offloading and problem-solving.

Additional research might also explore how the relationship between dependence and cognitive performance shifts after structured GenAI training and a comparison of students with varying degrees of AI literacy.

items.abstract_text: This paper explores how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital labour affect marginalised identities, using the 2025 Netflix film Humans in the Loop (directed by Aranya Sahay). Research follows the female protagonist of the film, named Nehma, an Indigenous (Adivasi) woman who works as a data labeller. Her deep, traditional knowledge about nature is ignored because of the way AI categorisation systems use a rigid, one-size-fits-all sorting method and act as epistemic hierarchies that erase Indigenous ways of living and thinking. Using a social semiotic approach, the research identifies a disconnection between local ecological knowledge and the rigid binary logic of machine-learning infrastructures. The article argues that digital frameworks mirror power dynamics inside educational institutions, where underrepresented students often have their cultural identity and cultural expressions erased or misrepresented. By analysing the lived experiences of marginalised communities, the study critiques techno-solutionist solutions and proposes solutions grounded in epistemic justice, cultural agency and equity and recommends that equitable AI systems require moving away from extractive labour practices to recognise the intellectual and cultural contributions of the Global South.

items.abstract_text: The Metacognitive Creative Destruction (MCD) model approaches educational innovation as a perpetual spiral process. Contradiction (accumulated cognitive conflicts that resist interpretation), activates Metacognitive Capacity, enabling Destructive Unlearning Propensity, the conscious abandonment of outdated mental schemas, which in turn enables Creative Reconstruction Ability, and ultimately, new knowledge. In the model’s empirical validation with 1,498 teachers, a critical finding emerged: AI Augmentation Intensity (AIA) predicted Metacognitive Capacity (MC) and Creative Reconstruction Ability (CRA), but not Destructive Unlearning Propensity (DUP).This article argues that this finding is not accidental, but reflects an inherent weakness of modern AI systems, and more specifically, the tendency toward AI Sycophancy. Models trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) tend to avoid disagreements and be likable to the user, preventing the individual from experiencing cognitive conflicts, perpetuating their already formed beliefs at the expense of scientific accuracy.Therefore, in an environment of “algorithmic flattery”, the necessary contradictions that trigger unlearning are not produced. Based on the MCD model, it is concluded that the absence of unlearning, that is, the deliberate and conscious abandonment of outdated beliefs, mental models and practices, makes the reconstruction of knowledge absolutely superficial and thus, algorithmically condescending interaction does not produce deep and authentic knowledge, regardless of AI Augmentation Intensity.

items.abstract_text: Background As Taiwan enters a super-aged society, the prevalence of dementia continues to rise, highlighting the need for scalable, noninvasive approaches to identify behavioral alterations associated with cognitive decline. AI-based analysis of spontaneous affective facial responses has emerged as a potential digital phenotyping tool, but its feasibility for assessing cognitive performance remains underexplored. Objective This study aimed to examine the feasibility of using AI-derived spontaneous affective facial response metrics, including affective expression congruency and onset latency, to characterize differences across cognitive performance levels in older adults with healthy cognition (HC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), or dementia. Methods A total of 60 participants (HC, MCI, and dementia; 20 per group) were presented with positive and negative emotion-eliciting videos and completed Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) recall and calculation tasks. Facial expressions were video-recorded and analyzed using a convolutional neural network–based AI system. AI-derived metrics included affective expression congruency, categorized as congruent, neutral, or incongruent according to the detected facial response, and affective expression onset latency, defined as the time from stimulus presentation to the emergence of a nonneutral facial expression detected by the AI model. Group differences were analyzed using 1-way ANOVA, Pearson chi-square or Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact tests, Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise post hoc comparisons, analysis of covariance adjusting for age and education, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses. Results Affectively congruent responses were generally less frequent among participants with lower cognitive performance. During the 14-second positive stimulus, congruent positive expressions were observed in 65% (13/20) of HC participants, 20% (4/20) of MCI participants, and 0% (0/20) of participants with dementia. During the 48-second negative stimulus, congruent negative expressions were observed in 60% (12/20) of HC participants compared with 5% (1/20) of both MCI and dementia participants. Onset latency differed significantly across groups for the 14-second positive stimulus (F2,57=19.63; P<.001; η2=0.41), 52-second positive stimulus (F2,57=4.25; P=.02; η2=0.13), 48-second negative stimulus (F2,57=15.61; P<.001; η2=0.35), and MMSE-based cognitive-task condition (F2,57=11.28; P<.001; η2=0.28). After adjustment for age and education, the group effect remained significant for all latency outcomes (F2,55=3.89-10.68; all P≤.03; partial η2=0.12-0.28). Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses showed stronger separation in several HC vs MCI and HC vs dementia comparisons, whereas MCI vs dementia comparisons showed limited separability. Conclusions AI-assisted analysis of spontaneous affective facial responses revealed differences in expression congruency and onset latency across cognitive performance levels. These preliminary findings suggest that AI-derived facial behavioral metrics may serve as noninvasive adjunctive features for observational cognitive assessment. However, the findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the exploratory design, modest sample size, and absence of internal or external validation.

This study asks whether working from a large language model draft lowers cognitive load or merely redistributes it. Thirty-six translators, twenty translation trainees and sixteen practising professionals, rendered nine English popular-science and technical passages into Chinese under three within-subject conditions. These were unaided human translation (HT), post-editing of a static neural machine translation draft (NMT-PE), and post-editing of a GPT-4o draft with an interactive prompt pane (GAI-PE). Pupil diameter change, fixation duration, gaze distribution, keystroke logs, NASA-TLX ratings and MQM scores were recorded. GAI-PE cut task time by 44.2 per cent against HT and by 17.1 per cent against NMT-PE. Its MQM scores were higher than those of NMT-PE, while the difference from HT did not reach significance. Pupil diameter change was nevertheless largest in GAI-PE at 0.095 mm, against 0.083 mm in HT and 0.064 mm in NMT-PE, while gaze on the source text fell to 38.3 per cent, the lowest of the three. Subjective ratings moved the other way and ranked HT as the most demanding condition. In an exploratory analysis, self-reported AI-use frequency was associated with a smaller pupil response in GAI-PE, whereas English proficiency showed no such association. These observations are consistent with an increased demand for verification, though the generative condition also gave access to an interactive prompt pane, so the differences cannot be attributed to the model alone.'}

items.abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have made their way into English Language Teaching (ELT) contexts, yet their pedagogical value remains contested. While many learners engage with GenAI primarily as a quick hack for producing answers, fewer use it as a resource for reflective language learning. This study explores prompt writing as a language learning task that supports both language development and metacognitive awareness. The study was conducted with a target group of pre-seminary, tertiary-level learners with mixed linguistic proficiency. Over the course of four instructional sessions, the study used a classroom-based action research design. Learners engaged in cycles of prompt drafting, GenAI-generated responses, peer discussion, and prompt refinement. Classroom observations, learner reflections, and group discussions were used to gather qualitative insights. The findings indicate measurable improvement in learners’ autonomy, as learners became aware of how lexical choices shape meaning, along with increased engagement, teamwork, and reflective thinking. The study argues that prompt writing, when treated as a language task rather than a technical skill, can function as a practical tool for fostering metacognition in ELT classrooms.

items.abstract_text: The article develops a psycholinguistic account of how generative artificial intelligence changes professional Ukrainian-language writing, with particular attention to language norms, professional speech etiquette, communicative culture, and the educational workplace. A structured theoretical synthesis was conducted on a corpus of 29 peer-reviewed journal articles from 2022–2026. The corpus was organised into four evidence blocks: artificial intelligence in business and workplace communication; pragmatic behaviour of large language models; politeness and email communication in academic and workplace settings; and Ukrainian psycholinguistic and speech-etiquette contexts. Studies were coded for communication domain, speech act or genre, role of artificial intelligence, normative and pragmatic outcomes, relational perceptions, and contextual limitations. Because research designs and outcome measures were heterogeneous, the analysis used qualitative comparative synthesis rather than meta-analysis. The synthesis reveals three recurrent transformations. First, generative systems often strengthen formal correctness, structural coherence, and explicit politeness. Second, these gains can be accompanied by communicative conventionalisation: increased formality, formulaic organisation, reduced lexical or strategic variability, and weaker adjustment to the local interpersonal context. Third, artificial-intelligence mediation changes attributional and relational judgements: perceived authorship, authenticity, sincerity, trust, and willingness to maintain interaction may diverge from ratings of professionalism or clarity. These transformations are not uniform; their magnitude depends on communicative risk, status relations, degree of imposition, genre conventionality, source disclosure, and the extent of human revision. On this basis, a three-component model of normative optimisation, communicative conventionalisation, and attributional-relational shift is proposed. For Ukrainian professional communication, especially in higher education, generative artificial intelligence should be treated as a mediator of linguistic choice rather than a neutral editing device. The key research gap is the lack of direct empirical evidence on Ukrainian-language AI-mediated professional writing, which limits straightforward transfer of findings from English-dominant studies.

reading.interpretation: AI can expand practice and feedback opportunities in clinical reasoning education, with selected studies showing favorable short-term outcomes across VP practice, orthopedic knowledge tasks, and automated feedback. Across these domains, the decisive question is whether supported performance develops into durable, unaided reasoning. Never-skilling is therefore best treated as a testable training outcome alongside retention, transfer, error detection, and calibration. AI-augmented cognitive apprenticeship translates this question into a practical design for prospective evaluation. items.abstract_text: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) increasingly mediates product search, evaluation, and choice, consumer cognition is becoming distributed across human–AI systems. This shift challenges a largely unexamined assumption in advertising theory: that persuasion operates through cognitive elaboration within the individual consumer. Drawing on cognitive offloading research from cognitive psychology, we develop the CogOffload framework to explain when consumers delegate cognitive work to Gen-AI and what consequences follow.
